content:
Architecture GPUStack Operator schedules accelerator workloads on Kubernetes. It discovers node hardware and builds isolated Kueue scheduling pools for Instances, ModelDeployments, and Pods. Model delivery resolves and caches weights, topology placement constrains failure domains, remote direct memory access (RDMA) accelerates transfers, and shared KV cache stores reusable prefixes.
Contents Components Workload flow Device scheduling Vocabulary Related documentation Components The gpustack-operator binary provides five subcommands, paired with the engine-sentinel runtime package staged into managed inference Pods:
Component Deployment Role worker Control-plane Deployment Serves APIs and reconciles workloads, queues, and supporting resources. device-manager Vendor DaemonSet Discovers accelerators and NICs,
publishes capacity, and allocates devices. model-manager Per-node DaemonSet Caches verified model weights and mounts them through CSI. model-transfer Vendor source DaemonSet Runs the source broker and worker service, paired with the staged gpustack_model_transfer Python reader package for remote weight delivery. worker-gateway Separate installation Aggregates InstanceTypes and capacity across clusters into one fleet view. engine-sentinel Read-only host mount in engine Pods Pure-Python runtime package (gpustack_engine_sentinel) for live parameter tuning, unified /gpustack/v1/{live,ready} probes, role pause, and PreStop drain; see Online Runtime Control . The Helm chart bundles Node Feature Discovery (NFD) , Kueue , and two CSI drivers. Topograph is optional and disabled until an administrator configures a topology provider. See Installation Modes for deployment modes and runtime settings.
Workload flow GPU Instances run interactive containers with optional SSH access. ModelDeployments run managed inference roles, routers, and prefill/decode (PD) or encode/prefill/decode (EPD) groups. Both consume the same pool capacity and admission chain, while model delivery and KV cache attach only when requested.
Every optional service in the diagram can be omitted. An ordinary Pod can also request accelerator resources directly through its namespace LocalQueue.
Model delivery A ModelArtifact separates weight sources and credentials from workload specs. It resolves and pins weights from Hugging Face, ModelScope, an OCI image, or a PersistentVolumeClaim.
Workloads load weights directly in the engine (Engine), mount verified node cache paths through the Model Manager CSI driver (Node), or mount an image or PVC. Remote delivery streams weights from prepared source nodes through model-transfer; see Remote Weight Delivery .
ModelStore and ModelStoreBinding govern node selection and namespace cache quotas. NodeModelStore reports per-node cache state, and ModelPrefetch warms weights ahead of serving without holding GPU quota. See Model Delivery , Model Artifact , and the Model Prefetch Walkthrough .
KV cache A KVCacheBackend deploys a shared Mooncake cache cluster or connects to an external endpoint. KVCachePool and KVCachePoolBinding grant namespace access, reuse domains, and memory ceilings independently of GPU quota. Compatible ModelDeployments and labeled Pods receive client settings at creation; see KV Cache .
Model Deployment combines these capabilities with engine, router, and scaling policies. GPU Instances run interactive containers on the same accelerator pools.
Device scheduling Device scheduling runs in four stages:
NFD inspects node hardware and publishes feature labels. Device Manager detects accelerators and NICs and updates each node’s Devices ledger. The worker derives schedulable CPU and accelerator capacity labels from that inventory. The worker creates an AcceleratorType per accelerated pool (plus InstanceTypes when enabled) sharing one isolated ClusterQueue. Heterogeneous Devices and Preflight Checks cover node readiness and isolation modes. Accelerator Requests defines resource keys, capacity views, and pool selection. See RDMA Operations for fabric requests and Topology-Aware Scheduling Operations for domain placement.
Request admission The Pod webhook validates accelerator requests before Kueue reserves quota. Kueue AdmissionChecks verify per-device fit and multi-role gang readiness before kube-scheduler, kubelet, and the allocator bind devices; see Accelerator Requests .
AcceleratorType and InstanceType status update as workloads claim and release accelerators. Run kubectl get acctype,instancetype -w to watch live pool capacity, or follow the Heterogeneous Devices Walkthrough .
Vocabulary Term Meaning Pool Nodes with matching CPU, accelerator, OS, and architecture identities, served by one isolated ClusterQueue. AcceleratorType Cluster-scoped accelerator pool for serving and prefetch workloads; short name acctype. InstanceType Cluster-scoped workspace sizing and capacity view for Instances. Allocation mode Whole cards, shared cards, logical slices, or hardware partitions. Credits Quota units (credits.gpustack.ai/<manufacturer>) metered on a pool ClusterQueue. Four capacity views Exclusive (EX), shared (SH), sliced (SL), and partitioned (PT) counts on pool status. Devices ledger Per-node custom resource recording discovered hardware and active allocations. LocalQueue Namespace queue entrance that routes a workload into its target ClusterQueue. ModelArtifact Namespaced weight source and resolved manifest digest referenced by workloads. NodeModelStore Per-node cache configuration and observed digest state. ModelPrefetch Namespaced request to warm a ModelArtifact onto bound ModelStore nodes. A physical card or module is a device, each schedulable unit on it is an accelerator, and the Kubernetes extended resource key a container requests is a resource.
Related documentation Heterogeneous Devices Walkthrough : submit workloads and inspect pool updates. GPU Instances : launch interactive containers with SSH access. Model Deployment : configure inference engines, routers, and scalers. Model Delivery : resolve, prefetch, and mount model weights. KV Cache : attach workloads to shared prefix caches. Installation Modes : compare chart mode, image mode, and settings precedence. See also — Accelerator Requests (resource keys and request rules) · Vendor Prerequisites (host drivers and third-party components)
Next → Heterogeneous Devices Walkthrough — follow a workload from submission to allocation.
title: Architecture

content:
Vendor Prerequisites Install the manufacturer driver and any required container toolkit before installing GPUStack. If a vendor GPU Operator runs on the same nodes, disable competing device plugins, node labellers, and duplicate NFD instances first. Vendor chart keys vary by release, so check the version cited in each section.
Contents Third-party dependencies Vendor setup requirements Shared cluster requirements Third-party dependencies Review these cluster dependencies before installing GPUStack. Ownership rules for chart mode and image mode are in Installation Modes .
Dependency Role Configuration Node Feature Discovery (NFD) Labels Nodes and publishes hardware features. Run one NFD master per cluster. See Single NFD per cluster . Kueue Manages workload quota and gang admission. Bundled in the chart; see Installation Modes . Topograph Publishes topology domains from a provider. Optional and disabled by default. See Topology-Aware Scheduling Operations . Mooncake Provides KV cache storage and transfer transport. Optional. Match engine, client, store, and transport in Engine Compatibility . ModelExpress Coordinates NVIDIA peer weight transfer and cache sharing. Optional; the operator creates a per-deployment metadata service. See ModelExpress . CSI drivers Mount NFS or S3 volumes, or mount cached weights. NFS and S3 ship as bundled subcharts; node model delivery uses Model Manager CSI (Model Store Operations ). Serving engines Run inference containers. Select a compatible runner image from Engine Compatibility . Vendor drivers and toolkits Expose accelerators to node workloads. Install host prerequisites from Vendor setup requirements . Vendor setup requirements AMD Checked against AMD GPU Operator v1.5.1 (Overview · Helm Chart Install · Toolkit Install ).
Install before GPUStack — install only the ROCm kernel driver. Per Container toolkit requirements , GPUStack injects /dev/kfd and each granted card’s DRM nodes directly, so neither AMD Container Toolkit nor amd-container-runtime is needed.
If a workload runs as non-root, add video and render to its container securityContext supplementary groups. Kubernetes device plugins cannot grant supplementary groups. Without those groups, ROCm enumerates zero agents without raising an error; verify inside the container with rocminfo rather than sysfs-based rocm-smi.
Vendor GPU Operator — AMD GPU Operator reconciles a DeviceConfig custom resource created by its Helm chart. Disable its device plugin and node labeller on DeviceConfig, and disable bundled NFD and Kernel Module Management (when drivers are pre-installed) in Helm values:
yamlCopy apiVersion: amd.com/v1alpha1 kind: DeviceConfig metadata: name: default namespace: kube-amd-gpu spec: driver: enable: true # default: true metricsExporter: enable: true # default: false devicePlugin: enableDevicePlugin: false # disable: conflicts with GPUStack amd.com/gpu plugin enableNodeLabeller: false # disable: GPUStack publishes capacity labels draDriver: enable: true # optional: mutually exclusive with devicePlugin on one DeviceConfig yamlCopy node-feature-discovery: enabled: false # disable: run one NFD per cluster kmm: enabled: false # disable when ROCm driver is pre-installed on the host watch: false Install it — install the chart with NFD and KMM disabled, then patch the chart-created DeviceConfig:
bashCopy helm repo add rocm https://rocm.github.io/gpu-operator helm repo update helm install amd-gpu-operator rocm/gpu-operator-charts \ --namespace kube-amd-gpu --create-namespace \ --version=v1.5.1 \ --set node-feature-discovery.enabled=false \ --set kmm.enabled=false \ --set kmm.watch=false kubectl -n kube-amd-gpu patch deviceconfig <name> --type merge -p \ '{"spec":{"devicePlugin":{"enableDevicePlugin":false,"enableNodeLabeller":false},"metricsExporter":{"enable":true}}}' The patch applies this change to the existing DeviceConfig:
diffCopy apiVersion: amd.com/v1alpha1 kind: DeviceConfig metadata: name: <name> namespace: kube-amd-gpu spec: devicePlugin: - enableDevicePlugin: true - enableNodeLabeller: true + enableDevicePlugin: false + enableNodeLabeller: false metricsExporter: - enable: false + enable: true Already installed — both plugins advertise amd.com/gpu. Stop the vendor plugin before installing GPUStack:
Device plugin and Node Labeller: patch the existing DeviceConfig as shown above. Do not delete the DaemonSet directly, because the operator recreates it from DeviceConfig. Bundled NFD: if the release enabled NFD, run helm upgrade with its existing values plus --set node-feature-discovery.enabled=false. Verify: wait until kubectl get node <node> -o jsonpath='{.status.allocatable}' no longer lists amd.com/gpu before installing GPUStack. Ascend Checked against the Ascend NPU driver and firmware (Driver Install ) and ascend-docker-runtime 26.1.0 on Atlas A5 (950 series).
Install before GPUStack — install the Ascend NPU driver, firmware, and Ascend Docker Runtime. Per Container toolkit requirements , GPUStack sets ASCEND_VISIBLE_DEVICES without /dev nodes, so the runtime hook must mount the devices. Register the runtime under handler ascend (matching the chart’s RuntimeClass), or set deviceManager.createRuntimeClasses=false and supply your own.
On Atlas A5 (950), install ascend-docker-runtime newer than 26.0.x1. Releases 7.3.x and earlier support 910B and older generations only. On A5, an older runtime does not recognize Ascend950, falls back to legacy manager devices, and fails container creation on missing /dev/devmm_svm.
Do not rely on ascend-docker-runtime --version; the wrapper forwards --version to host runc. Read the installer metadata file instead:
bashCopy grep '^version=' /usr/local/Ascend/Ascend-Docker-Runtime/ascend_docker_runtime_install.info # version=v7.3.0 <- predates A5 support # version=v26.1.0 <- serves A5 gpustack-operator device-manager preflight checks the same file and reports it as ascend-docker-runtime on each A5 NPU.
A5 host ranktable — on Atlas A5 (950), /etc/hccl_rootinfo.json must be absent (default) or at version "2.0". Prefer ascend-docker-runtime 26.2+ so the runtime does not mount it unconditionally. If an A2 ("1.0") or A3 ("1.2") ranktable remains on the host, libhccl_v2 fails multi-card jobs with Config_Error_Ranktable (EI0014):
bashCopy # absent is healthy; HCCL negotiates through rootInfo test -e /etc/hccl_rootinfo.json && grep -o '"version"[^,]*' /etc/hccl_rootinfo.json # "version": "1.0" <- breaks multi-card HCCL on A5; remove or regenerate as 2.0 Preflight reports this state as hccl-ranktable .
A5 conditional host mounts — on Ascend A5 (status.detail.family "950"), device-manager inspects /etc/hccl_rootinfo.json (regular non-symlink file <= 1 MiB at version "2.0") and /lib/route.conf (regular non-symlink file) through /host during Allocate and mounts valid files read-only. Absent, symlinked, invalid, or colliding paths are skipped cleanly, non-A5 hosts never receive either mount, and deviceManager.hostRootMount.enabled=false disables both.
A5 Host RoCE endpoints — for Ascend A5 Host RoCE (roce:host) vLLM workloads, create per-NPU endpoint files at /etc/hixlep/ub_endpoint_npu_<physical_id>.json on every Host RoCE node. Managed Host RoCE Pods mount /etc/hixlep read-only (HostPathDirectory); a missing directory blocks kubelet volume setup, and a missing file fails vllm-ascend with FileNotFoundError. See Ascend A5 topologies .
Cambricon Checked against Cambricon driver 5.10.22 (Neuware SDK 1.15.0, Driver Install ).
Install before GPUStack — install only the Cambricon MLU driver. Per Container toolkit requirements , GPUStack injects card and host control /dev nodes on both whole-card and sliced allocations and sets CAMBRICON_VISIBLE_DEVICES for compatibility with cambricon-container-runtime, so cntoolkit is not required.
Hygon Checked against Hygon DCU Operator (latest unversioned vendor docs, Overview ).
Install before GPUStack — install the Hygon DCU driver and firmware so /dev/kfd, /dev/mkfd, /dev/dri/card*, and /dev/dri/renderD* exist on the host. Per Container toolkit requirements , GPUStack injects those device nodes directly without a container toolkit.
Vendor GPU Operator — Hygon DCU Operator configures all components on one DeviceConfig custom resource (kubectl explain deviceconfig.spec). Substitute the cluster’s installed apiVersion and object name:
yamlCopy apiVersion: <existing-api-version> kind: DeviceConfig metadata: name: device-config namespace: kube-system spec: metricsExporter: enable: true # default: false dcgm: enable: true # default: false devicePlugin: enableDevicePlugin: false # disable: conflicts with GPUStack hygon.com/dcu plugin enableNodeLabeller: false # disable: DCU-Label-Node conflicts with GPUStack labels Install it — after installing the operator from Hygon’s portal, patch its DeviceConfig:
bashCopy kubectl -n kube-system patch deviceconfig <name> --type merge -p \ '{"spec":{"devicePlugin":{"enableDevicePlugin":false,"enableNodeLabeller":false},"metricsExporter":{"enable":true},"dcgm":{"enable":true}}}' Read apiVersion and metadata.name from kubectl get deviceconfig -n kube-system -o yaml:
diffCopy apiVersion: <existing-api-version> kind: DeviceConfig metadata: name: <name> namespace: kube-system spec: devicePlugin: - enableDevicePlugin: <current-value> + enableDevicePlugin: false - enableNodeLabeller: <current-value> + enableNodeLabeller: false metricsExporter: - enable: <current-value> + enable: true dcgm: - enable: <current-value> + enable: true Already installed — both plugins advertise hygon.com/dcu. Stop the vendor plugin first:
Device plugin and DCU-Label-Node: apply the DeviceConfig patch above. Do not delete the DaemonSets directly. Verify: wait until hygon.com/dcu disappears from Node allocatable capacity before installing GPUStack. Iluvatar Checked against ix-GPU-Operator v4.4.0 and ix-Container-Toolkit v1.1.0 (Helm Chart Install · Toolkit Install ).
Install before GPUStack — install matching versions of the Iluvatar driver and ix-Container-Toolkit (for example, driver v4.4.0 with toolkit v1.1.0). Per Container toolkit requirements , GPUStack sets IX_VISIBLE_DEVICES without /dev nodes. Register the runtime as iluvatar, or set deviceManager.createRuntimeClasses=false and supply your own RuntimeClass.
Vendor GPU Operator — ix-GPU-Operator exposes one Helm value per component:
yamlCopy ixDriver: enabled: false # default: false; keep off when driver is pre-installed ixExporter: enabled: true # default: true ixDevicePlugin: enabled: false # disable: conflicts with GPUStack iluvatar.com/gpu plugin ixfd: enabled: false # disable: bundles upstream NFD Install it — install the OCI chart with the competing components disabled:
bashCopy helm install --wait ix-gpu-operator \ oci://registry.iluvatar.com.cn:10443/k8s/ix-gpu-operator --version 1.0.0 \ --create-namespace --namespace ix-gpu-operator \ --insecure-skip-tls-verify \ --set global.repository="registry.iluvatar.com.cn/k8s" \ --set global.version=4.4.0 \ --set ixDriver.enabled=false \ --set ixDevicePlugin.enabled=false \ --set ixfd.enabled=false Already installed — both plugins advertise iluvatar.com/gpu. Stop ix-Device-Plugin first:
ix-Device-Plugin and ix-Feature-Discovery: run helm upgrade with existing values plus --set ixDevicePlugin.enabled=false --set ixfd.enabled=false. Verify: wait until iluvatar.com/gpu leaves Node allocatable capacity before installing GPUStack. On software stacks older than v4.3.0, ix-GPU-Operator ships as static YAML without component switches. Delete that manifest and install the host driver and ix-Container-Toolkit directly.
MetaX Checked against MetaX Kubernetes GPU Operator v0.15.3 (Overview · Helm Chart Install · Components ).
Install before GPUStack — install the MetaX driver and MXMACA SDK on the host. Per Container toolkit requirements , GPUStack injects /dev/mxcd, /dev/mxnd, /dev/mxgd, and card DRM nodes directly, so no container toolkit is required.
Vendor GPU Operator — MetaX GPU Operator marks gpu-device and gpu-label mandatory in every mode, including minimalMode:
Component Action Mechanism Kernel driver and MXMACA SDK Keep on host --set minimalMode=true leaves both to the host mx-exporter Optional Optional under minimalMode controller-exporter Optional Optional under minimalMode gpu-device (device plugin) Cannot disable Mandatory in every vendor install mode gpu-label (NFD-equivalent) Cannot disable Mandatory in every vendor install mode gpu-scheduler Disable Leave undeployed topo-discovery Disable Leave undeployed Install it — minimalMode is fixed at install time and only fits nodes that GPUStack does not manage:
bashCopy helm install oci://DOMAIN/PROJECT/metax-operator \ --version VERSION \ --create-namespace -n metax-operator \ --generate-name \ --wait \ --set registry=DOMAIN/PROJECT \ --set minimalMode=true Already installed — because gpu-device cannot be disabled and advertises metax-tech.com/gpu, the vendor operator and GPUStack cannot share a node:
Host driver and MXMACA SDK: confirm both are installed on the host outside the operator so uninstalling the chart does not remove them. Uninstall release: run helm uninstall on the MetaX operator release. Verify: wait until metax-tech.com/gpu leaves Node allocatable capacity before installing GPUStack. Moore Threads Checked against MT GPU Operator v2.1.0 (KUAE Cloud Native, Overview · Helm Chart Install ).
Install before GPUStack — install the Moore Threads driver and MT Container Toolkit. Per Container toolkit requirements , GPUStack sets MTHREADS_VISIBLE_DEVICES without /dev nodes.
Vendor GPU Operator — MT GPU Operator ships two modes: full (two Helm charts whose controller always reconciles the vendor device plugin with no disable switch) and core (plain YAML manifests containing only the device plugin and exporter):
yamlCopy mtGpuClusterPolicyClusterpolicy: driverToolkit: enabled: true # default: true containerToolkit: enabled: true # default: true dcgm: enabled: true dcgmExporter: enabled: true nfd: enabled: false # disable: run one NFD per cluster gpuScheduler: enabled: false # default: false gpuWebhook: enabled: false # default: false kured: enabled: false nodeProblemDetector: enabled: false aiOps: enabled: false Install it — full mode below suits nodes left to the vendor plugin; for nodes managed by GPUStack, install host drivers and MT Container Toolkit directly and apply core manifests with the device plugin removed:
bashCopy helm install --wait mt-gpu-operator mt-gpu-operator helm install --wait mt-gpu-operator-custom-resources mt-gpu-operator-custom-resources \ --set mtGpuClusterPolicyClusterpolicy.nfd.enabled=false \ --set mtGpuClusterPolicyClusterpolicy.kured.enabled=false \ --set mtGpuClusterPolicyClusterpolicy.nodeProblemDetector.enabled=false \ --set mtGpuClusterPolicyClusterpolicy.aiOps.enabled=false Already installed — both plugins advertise mthreads.com/gpu. Stop the vendor plugin before installing GPUStack:
Cluster add-ons: in full mode, upgrade mt-gpu-operator-custom-resources with the false flags above (core mode deploys none of them). Device plugin: full mode: uninstall both Helm charts, ensure the driver and MT Container Toolkit remain on the host, and switch to core mode if you still want the exporter. core mode: remove the device plugin from deployments.yaml, keep the exporter, and re-apply. Verify: wait until mthreads.com/gpu leaves Node allocatable capacity before installing GPUStack. NVIDIA Checked against NVIDIA GPU Operator v26.3.3 (Overview · Helm Chart Install ).
Install before GPUStack — install the NVIDIA driver and NVIDIA Container Toolkit (either on the host or via NVIDIA GPU Operator). Per Container toolkit requirements , GPUStack sets NVIDIA_VISIBLE_DEVICES by default or emits CDI annotations; both paths require the toolkit.
Device Manager also relies on the toolkit for MIG management (NVIDIA_MIG_CONFIG_DEVICES and NVIDIA_MIG_MONITOR_DEVICES); see MIG prerequisites .
Vendor GPU Operator — keep the driver, toolkit, DCGM exporter, and GPU Feature Discovery, and disable components that conflict with GPUStack:
yamlCopy driver: enabled: true # default: true toolkit: enabled: true # default: true dcgmExporter: enabled: true # default: true devicePlugin: enabled: false # disable: conflicts with GPUStack nvidia.com/gpu plugin gfd: enabled: true # default: true nfd: enabled: false # disable, or keep and disable GPUStack bundled NFD migManager: enabled: false # disable: conflicts with Allocate-time MIG actuation cdi: enabled: false # default: true from v25.10; disable on MIG nodes For the single-profile exception where fleet-wide MIG Manager can stay enabled, see Fleet-wide MIG Manager . Also verify that managed nodes do not carry nvidia.com/gpu.deploy.operands=false; that label suppresses all operands while ClusterPolicy still reports ready.
Install it — install the chart with the competing components disabled:
bashCopy helm repo add nvidia https://helm.ngc.nvidia.com/nvidia helm repo update helm install --wait --generate-name \ -n gpu-operator --create-namespace \ nvidia/gpu-operator --version=v26.3.3 \ --set devicePlugin.enabled=false \ --set nfd.enabled=false \ --set migManager.enabled=false \ --set cdi.enabled=false Already installed — run one helm upgrade preserving existing values plus the switches below (do not delete DaemonSets manually, or ClusterPolicy recreates them):
Device plugin: pass --set devicePlugin.enabled=false. MIG Manager: pass --set migManager.enabled=false. Existing geometry stays intact until GPUStack reconfigures partitions at Allocate time. Bundled NFD: pass --set nfd.enabled=false (GPUStack’s bundled NFD already publishes the system-os_release.* labels NVIDIA’s operator expects), or see Single NFD per cluster to keep NVIDIA’s NFD instead. CDI on MIG nodes: pass --set cdi.enabled=false on nodes serving MIG. Verify: wait until nvidia.com/gpu leaves Node allocatable capacity before installing GPUStack. CDI mode — --set cdi.enabled=false gives GPUStack end-to-end control; leaving CDI on works only for non-MIG whole-GPU nodes.
Why — GPU Operator v25.10+ defaults cdi.enabled: true (ignoring deprecated cdi.default). In CDI mode, the runtime resolves NVIDIA_VISIBLE_DEVICES against static /etc/cdi or /var/run/cdi specs, which never list MIG instances created dynamically at Allocate time.
Device injection channel — leave GPUSTACK_NVIDIA_DEVICE_INJECTION_STRATEGY at auto.
Why — auto selects cdi-annotations only when the Pod sets no runtimeClassName, the runtime config enables CDI on a non-vendor default handler, and CDI specs list every granted GPU; otherwise it falls back to envvar (NVIDIA_VISIBLE_DEVICES). When a Pod or Instance sets runtimeClassName: nvidia, that runtime handler performs injection directly.
T-Head Checked against T-Head SAIL SDK (PPU SDK, HGGCRT v3, Driver Install · Overview ).
Install before GPUStack — install the PPU SDK Runfile (/usr/local/PPU_SDK by default) using HGGCRT v3 (backward compatible with v2), and verify with ppu-smi and hgcc --version. Per Container toolkit requirements , GPUStack injects /dev/alixpu, /dev/alixpu_ctl, and /dev/alixpu_ppu<N> (plus MIG partition nodes) directly without a vendor container runtime.
Shared cluster requirements Container toolkit requirements Whether a host needs a vendor container toolkit depends on what GPUStack’s allocator returns to kubelet:
Manufacturer Allocator injection Toolkit required AMD /dev nodes (/dev/kfd, /dev/dri/card*, /dev/dri/renderD*) No Ascend ASCEND_VISIBLE_DEVICES Yes Cambricon /dev nodes (/dev/cambricon_dev* and control nodes) plus CAMBRICON_VISIBLE_DEVICES No Hygon /dev nodes (/dev/kfd, /dev/mkfd, /dev/dri/card*, /dev/dri/renderD*) No Iluvatar IX_VISIBLE_DEVICES Yes MetaX /dev nodes (/dev/mxcd, /dev/mxnd, /dev/mxgd, /dev/dri/card*, /dev/dri/renderD*) No Moore Threads MTHREADS_VISIBLE_DEVICES Yes NVIDIA NVIDIA_VISIBLE_DEVICES by default, or CDI annotations (NVIDIA ) Yes T-Head /dev nodes (/dev/alixpu, /dev/alixpu_ctl, /dev/alixpu_ppu<N>) No Why — runc mounts returned /dev nodes directly, whereas an environment variable requires a vendor runtime hook to mount devices. Without that toolkit, the container starts with the variable set and zero accelerators visible.
Device plugin name collisions Kubelet allows a second device plugin to overwrite an existing registration for the same resource key. Node capacity then oscillates between both plugins, and Allocate calls fail when kubelet sends one plugin’s device IDs to the other. Stop competing vendor plugins before deploying GPUStack.
Single NFD per cluster Run exactly one NFD master per cluster. Two masters garbage-collect each other’s feature.node.kubernetes.io/* labels, which can remove pci-<vendor>.present labels and unschedule Device Manager DaemonSets.
GPUStack’s bundled NFD evaluates cluster-scoped NodeFeatureRules (such as AMD’s) and publishes system-os_release.* labels (required by NVIDIA GPU Operator).
Bringing your own NFD — disable GPUStack’s bundled NFD with --set node-feature-discovery.enabled=false in chart mode or --disable-applications=node-feature-discovery in image mode (Installation Modes ). The worker still applies gpustack-cpu-info, so the existing NFD installation must satisfy six rules:
Enable pci worker discovery with vendor in deviceLabelFields and PCI classes 02, 03, 0b, and 12 whitelisted2. Enable system worker discovery (system-os_release.*) if NVIDIA GPU Operator runs on the cluster. Evaluate NodeFeature objects from all namespaces so <node>-gpustack-* objects reach Nodes. Set restrictions.denyNodeFeatureLabels: false and disableExtendedResources: false. Allow acceleratable.feature.gpustack.ai and general.feature.gpustack.ai in denyLabelNs. Keep a single Helm release owning the NFD CRDs (both GPUStack and NVIDIA vendor NFD 0.19.0). Resource removal lag Disabling a vendor device plugin does not clear its extended resource from Node.status.allocatable instantaneously. Wait until kubelet reconverges and removes the vendor key before installing GPUStack.
Device Manager host mount deviceManager.hostRootMount.enabled defaults to true and mounts host / read-only (HostPathDirectory) at /host on the device-manager main container only (never on stage-libs). The host reader enforces three boundaries:
Root confinement: os.OpenRoot confines lookups under etc, proc, and usr. Read-only access: files open with O_RDONLY and os.SameFile checks, with zero write or exec paths. Symlink safety: intermediate symlinks resolve inside /host, while A5 regular-file checks reject leaf symlinks. Set deviceManager.hostRootMount.enabled=false when cluster policy forbids hostPath: / mounts or when custom ascend-docker-runtime setups should skip A5 conditional host mounts under Ascend .
See also — Preflight Checks (verify driver paths and runtime isolation on a node) · Heterogeneous Devices (device families and requests) · NVIDIA MIG Operations (MIG prerequisites and mode lifecycle)
Next → Installation Modes — choose chart or image ownership and runtime settings precedence.
Basic Atlas A5 support first shipped in ascend-docker-runtime 26.0.0 (noted as Atlas 350 PCIe support), after version numbers jumped directly from 7.3.x to 26.x. ↩︎
NVIDIA GPU Operator’s bundled NFD whitelists only 0300 and 0302 under node-feature-discovery.worker.config.sources.pci, omitting 0b and 12 NPUs unless extended. ↩︎
title: Vendor Prerequisites

content:
Heterogeneous Devices GPUStack discovers GPUs, NPUs, MLUs, DCUs, and PPUs across nodes and exposes them through Kueue pool queues. Each manufacturer governs its extended resource name and slicing or partitioning mechanism.
Contents Overview Configuration Operations Troubleshooting Overview Device Manager detects node hardware and updates the Devices ledger. The worker builds AcceleratorType pools (for serving and prefetch) and InstanceType pools (for interactive workspaces) over shared canonical ClusterQueues, while Kueue and the device plugin enforce quota and container isolation.
Configuration Accelerator requests Choose whole-card, shared, logically sliced, or hardware-partitioned resource keys in Accelerator Requests . Review the seven Pod validation rules in Request rules and pool capabilities in Isolation mode selection .
Operations Step 1: Run host preflight Run Preflight Checks on bare hosts before installing workloads.
Step 2: Request devices Submit queued workloads following the Heterogeneous Devices Walkthrough .
Step 3: Verify allocation Inspect pool capacity and Workload reservations in Pool troubleshooting . For hardware partitions, follow the NVIDIA , Hygon , or T-Head MIG runbooks.
Troubleshooting Resolve webhook rejections, queued demand, and per-card fragmentation in Diagnosing Pending workloads . Interpret host probe verdicts in Result format , and follow each vendor MIG runbook for partition recovery.
See also — GPU Instances (interactive accelerator workspaces) · Architecture (end-to-end scheduling chain)
Next → Accelerator Requests — select resource keys and verify admission rules.
title: Heterogeneous Devices

content:
Hygon MIG Operations Administrators toggle Hygon DCU partitioning mode node-wide with hy-smi and restart the Device Manager DaemonSet to re-detect. Once enabled, GPUStack dynamically creates and destroys GPU and Compute Instance pairs for scheduled workloads under hygon.com/dcu.partitioned.mig-<profile> (Accelerator Requests ).
Contents Prerequisites Partition profile discovery Partition requests Operations Limitations Prerequisites Virtualization driver flag: Install the Hygon driver with virtualization support enabled; otherwise the driver exposes zero partition profiles.
Zero /dev/kfd holders (including Device Manager): hy-smi -mig fails with Set system level mig mode failed. The device is exist and may be in use. while any process (including the running Device Manager Pod) holds /dev/kfd (hymgr holding /dev/mkfd does not block). Verify empty output before switching:
bashCopy for p in /proc/[0-9]*; do pid=${p#/proc/}; n=$(ls -l "$p"/fd 2>/dev/null | grep -c kfd); \ [ "$n" -gt 0 ] 2>/dev/null && echo "pid=$pid fds=$n $(tr -d '\0' < "$p"/cmdline)"; done Device Manager restart: Restart gpustack-operator-device-manager-hygon after every mode change so Devices re-detects.
Partition profile discovery Device Manager queries supported profiles and legal placements directly from the driver (computing full-card CU counts from profile CUs × max instances while MIG mode is active). On a Hygon C-3000 “BW” DCU (4 slices, 80 CUs, 65520 MiB), the driver reports:
Profile Slices Compute units Memory Max per card Legal placements 2g.15gb 1 20 16380 MiB 4 0:1 1:1 2:1 3:1 4g.31gb 2 40 32760 MiB 2 0:2 2:2 8g.63gb 4 80 65520 MiB 1 0:4 Driver registry The Device Manager DaemonSet mounts /etc/dmi_mig_config writable so driver library calls can create and remove instance records, and reads dev<N> (PCI bus mapping) plus ci/dev<N>gi<G>ci<C>.conf (mig_uuid:) to bind partition handles back to physical cards.
Partition requests Request both hygon.com/dcu.partitioned: "1" and hygon.com/dcu.partitioned.mig-<profile>: "1" on a Kueue-labeled Pod (or set acceleratorPartitionedProfile on an Instance):
yamlCopy apiVersion: v1 kind: Pod metadata: name: hygon-partition namespace: team-a labels: kueue.x-k8s.io/queue-name: <local-queue> spec: containers: - name: main image: ubuntu:24.04 command: - sleep - "86400" resources: limits: hygon.com/dcu.partitioned: "1" hygon.com/dcu.partitioned.mig-2g.15gb: "1" requests: hygon.com/dcu.partitioned: "1" hygon.com/dcu.partitioned.mig-2g.15gb: "1" Device Manager carves the GPU/Compute Instance pair and injects /dev/kfd, /dev/mkfd, card DRM nodes, the user-space runtime, a read-only bind mount of /etc/dmi_mig_config/ci/dev<N>gi<G>ci<C>.conf at its exact host path, and DMI_MIG_VISIBLE_DEVICE=MIG-<uuid>.
Operations Enabling partitioning Consult the vendor DCU Multi-Instance manual (note: the long flag is --multi-instance-gpu, and -i is not supported):
Drain accelerator Pods, scale down or cordon gpustack-operator-device-manager-hygon on the Node, and verify zero /dev/kfd holders (Prerequisites ).
Enable node-wide MIG mode (do not pre-carve instances manually):
bashCopy sudo hy-smi -mig 1 Captured output:
textCopy Enabled mig mode successful. Restore and restart gpustack-operator-device-manager-hygon, then verify allocatable keys:
bashCopy kubectl get node <node> -o jsonpath='{.status.allocatable}' | tr ',' '\n' | grep hygon Captured output:
textCopy "hygon.com/dcu":"0" "hygon.com/dcu.partitioned":"32" "hygon.com/dcu.sliced":"0" Disabling partitioning Follow the strict teardown order required by the driver:
Drain all partition Pods and wait for automatic reclaim (or destroy manually per card, compute instances before GPU instances):
bashCopy sudo hy-smi mig -dci -i <card> sudo hy-smi mig -dgi -i <card> Stop gpustack-operator-device-manager-hygon on the Node so /dev/kfd is closed.
Disable node-wide MIG mode (sudo hy-smi -mig 0).
Start gpustack-operator-device-manager-hygon and confirm hygon.com/dcu and hygon.com/dcu.sliced return.
Node reboot recovery MIG instances and /etc/dmi_mig_config reset on host reboot. Verify hy-smi MIG mode after reboot, restart gpustack-operator-device-manager-hygon if needed, and recreate pre-reboot partition Pods (stale ownership markers are reclaimed automatically).
Limitations GPUStack creates and reclaims single-CI partition instances per Pod. It never toggles node-wide hy-smi -mig mode, mixes whole and partitioned DCUs on one Node, grants multiple partitions to one container, or keeps warm unclaimed partitions.
Node-wide, partition-only mode: hy-smi -mig takes no -i card flag. Once enabled, every card on the Node requires a MIG registry file (hygon.com/dcu and hygon.com/dcu.sliced drop to 0); mixed whole-card and partitioned DCUs on one Node are impossible. Single partition per container: The Hygon runtime exposes at most one partition per container regardless of DMI_MIG_VISIBLE_DEVICE; multi-partition workloads must use one Pod per partition. Registry directory poisoning: If a container starts after its .conf file was removed, the container runtime creates an empty directory at ci/dev<N>...conf, causing future creates to fail with INSUFFICIENT_RESOURCES. Current Device Manager builds sweep stray directories automatically (use rmdir manually on older builds). Ephemeral MIG UUIDs: Hygon generates a fresh mig_uuid on every create, even at the same slot. See also — Accelerator Requests (request rules and family split) · NVIDIA MIG Operations (per-GPU MIG runbook) · T-Head MIG Operations (PPU MIG runbook)

title: Hygon MIG Operations

content:
NVIDIA MIG Operations Administrators toggle NVIDIA Multi-Instance GPU (MIG) mode per GPU with nvidia-smi (or GPU Operator’s MIG Manager) and restart the node’s Device Manager DaemonSet to re-detect. Once MIG mode is active, GPUStack dynamically creates and destroys GPU/Compute Instance pairs for scheduled workloads.
MIG-enabled GPUs advertise nvidia.com/gpu.partitioned* keys exclusively, while unpartitioned GPUs on the same Node continue serving whole-GPU, shared, and logical-slice requests (Accelerator Requests ).
Contents Prerequisites Partition profile discovery Partition requests Operations MIG capacity scenarios Limitations Prerequisites The chart configures gpustack-operator-device-manager-nvidia with runtimeClassName: nvidia and NVIDIA_MIG_CONFIG_DEVICES / NVIDIA_MIG_MONITOR_DEVICES so NVML exposes MIG management (do not override these in deviceManager.env; see Vendor Prerequisites ).
Before toggling MIG mode on or off:
Drain workloads and driver handles: Stop all Pods on target GPUs and stop host daemons holding NVML handles (such as DCGM or nvsm) so the switch does not stay pending. Unload nvidia_drm and run with CAP_SYS_ADMIN: Loaded nvidia_drm blocks GPU resets. Generation reset rule: Ampere (A100/A30) requires a GPU reset (or VM reboot on passthrough hypervisors) after toggling MIG mode; Hopper (H100) and newer switch without a reset. Partition profile discovery Unlike T-Head and Hygon , NVIDIA MIG profiles come from a fixed per-product catalog matching NVIDIA’s Supported MIG Profiles (for example, 3g.20gb on A100-40GB and 3g.40gb on H100-80GB):
Excluded variants: Profiles containing + (+me, +me.all, +gfx) or lacking legal placement slots are omitted from the inventory. Whole GPU instances only: GPUStack creates one Compute Instance spanning the full GPU Instance; manually subdivided instances (nvidia-smi mig -cci) are refused. Placement-aware Remaining: Because profiles compete for fixed memory-slice intervals (for example, one 3g.40gb at 0–3 blocks the single 4g.40gb slot at 0–3 while leaving 4–7 free), Devices tracks both static profile ceilings and live Remaining counts. Partition requests Request one partitioned GPU and one exact profile on a Kueue-labeled Pod (.partitioned.units is derived automatically by the webhook):
yamlCopy apiVersion: v1 kind: Pod metadata: name: nvidia-partition namespace: team-a labels: kueue.x-k8s.io/queue-name: <local-queue> spec: containers: - name: main image: ubuntu:24.04 command: - sleep - "86400" resources: limits: nvidia.com/gpu.partitioned: "1" # always "1" nvidia.com/gpu.partitioned.mig-1g.10gb: "1" # always "1" Or request the profile on an Instance via spec.resources.acceleratorPartitionedProfile (mutually exclusive with slice percentages; host CPU/RAM scale by the profile’s VRAM share):
yamlCopy apiVersion: worker.gpustack.ai/v1 kind: Instance metadata: name: mig-instance namespace: team-a spec: type: gpustack--nvidia-h100-80gb-hbm3-linux-amd64 image: ubuntu:24.04 command: - sleep - "86400" resources: accelerator: "1" acceleratorPartitionedProfile: 3g.40gb volume: ephemeral: capacity: 1Gi Packing and reclaim: Device Manager bin-packs onto the most-occupied MIG GPU with a valid slot, keeping sibling GPUs free for wider profiles. On Pod exit, the reclaimer destroys the Compute Instance then the GPU Instance (retrying NVML_ERROR_IN_USE with bounded backoff). SSH sidecar isolation: On SSH-enabled Instances, the sshd sidecar verifies the on-disk ownership marker and MIG UUID under the GPU lock and receives only main’s MIG instance, never the parent GPU. Operations Enabling partitioning Satisfy Prerequisites , enable MIG mode per GPU or across all GPUs, and reset on Ampere:
bashCopy nvidia-smi -i <id> -mig 1 # or: nvidia-smi -mig 1 # On Ampere (A100/A30) only: nvidia-smi -i <id> -r Restart the NVIDIA Device Manager DaemonSet so the detector updates Devices in place (do not delete Devices or pre-carve instances):
bashCopy kubectl -n gpustack-system rollout restart ds/gpustack-operator-device-manager-nvidia kubectl -n gpustack-system rollout status ds/gpustack-operator-device-manager-nvidia Fleet-wide MIG Manager To toggle MIG mode declaratively through NVIDIA GPU Operator, enable --set migManager.enabled=true and label target Nodes with all-enabled (which enables MIG mode without pre-creating instances; never use all-balanced or all-1g.*):
bashCopy kubectl label node <node> nvidia.com/mig.config=all-enabled --overwrite Default all-disabled caution: Unlabeled Nodes default to all-disabled when MIG Manager starts, turning off hand-enabled MIG GPUs; ensure nvidia.com/mig.capable=true is present so MIG Manager schedules. Manual Device Manager restart still required: Restart gpustack-operator-device-manager-nvidia after MIG Manager finishes switching a Node (check nvidia-smi directly if masked DCGM causes nvidia.com/mig.config.state=failed). Disabling partitioning Drain partition Pods so instances reclaim (or destroy remaining instances manually), disable MIG mode, apply any Ampere reset, and restart gpustack-operator-device-manager-nvidia:
bashCopy nvidia-smi -i <id> -mig 0 # or: nvidia-smi -mig 0 Node reboot recovery After an unplanned reboot, re-run Enabling partitioning (including the Device Manager DaemonSet restart), then delete and recreate pre-reboot partition Pods so fresh MIG instances materialize.
MIG capacity scenarios Partitioning GPUs shifts capacity from EX/SH/SL to PT on InstanceType (SH below shows legacy 10-share display; current builds display card count 8/80 and 5/50, see Legacy request migration ). An 8-GPU H100-80GB Node reports these capacity views across three layouts:
Configuration Partitioned GPUs EX/SH/SL/PT Advertised node keys All-logical 0 of 8 8/8 80/80 100/800 0/0 Whole/shared + .sliced.* (1024 slices, 12800k units); .partitioned: 0 All-physical 8 of 8 0/0 0/0 0/0 1/56 .partitioned: 56 + .partitioned.mig-* (12800k units); logical keys 0 Mixed 3 of 8 5/5 50/50 100/500 1/21 5 GPUs under logical/whole (640 slices); 3 GPUs under .partitioned.* (21) Verification Wait for gpustack-operator-device-manager-nvidia to be Ready and .partitioned keys to register on the Node before submitting Pods, then verify carved UUIDs:
bashCopy kubectl get instancetypes gpustack--nvidia-h100-80gb-hbm3-linux-amd64 -o wide kubectl get node <node> -o json | jq '.status.allocatable | with_entries(select(.key|test("nvidia.com/gpu")))' kubectl exec <partition-pod> -- nvidia-smi -L kubectl get pod <partition-pod> -o jsonpath='{.metadata.annotations.device\.gpustack\.ai/accelerator\.allocated}{"\n"}' Captured output (1 × 3g.40gb carved on GPU 0):
textCopy GPU 0: NVIDIA H100 80GB HBM3 (UUID: GPU-950792bf-a01c-3f1a-e122-3473e67f54b2) MIG 3g.40gb Device 0: (UUID: MIG-b3061c09-2a4c-5026-a575-79f86a5bb12c) Capacity accounting When one live 3g.40gb occupies slices 0–3 on an 8-slice H100 (4–7 free), free start slots per profile on that GPU are:
Profile Slice width Legal starts Free starts Node key contribution 1g.10gb 1 0 1 2 3 4 5 6 4, 5, 6 3 1g.20gb 2 0 2 4 6 4, 6 2 2g.20gb 2 0 2 4 4 1 3g.40gb 4 0 4 4 1 allocated + 1 free 4g.40gb 4 0 — 0 7g.80gb 8 0 — 0 Across 7 empty GPUs plus that 1 carved GPU:
Surface Value Formula .partitioned.mig-<profile> 1g.10gb: 52, 3g.40gb: 16 Sum of allocated + remaining (scheduler subtracts live Pods) nvidia.com/gpu.partitioned 53 Sum of allocated + max(free profile count) per GPU InstanceType PT (onceMaxRequest/remaining) 1/52 1 while any slot is free; sum of max(free profile count) without allocated status.detail.slicedDetail reflects static empty-pool capability from Devices.spec; read PT and PARTITIONS (-o wide) for live remaining slots.
Limitations GPUStack creates and reclaims single-CI MIG instances for scheduled workloads and cleans idle untracked instances. It never toggles MIG mode, resets GPUs, evicts Pods on mode switches, or serves subdivided -cci instances.
No manual nvidia-smi mig -cgi or -cci: Hand-carved instances desynchronize node capacity keys and are destroyed as orphans once idle; subdivided -cci instances halt node-wide reclaim until removed. Immediate replacement race: Node capacity keys free on Pod deletion slightly ahead of debounced hardware destroy; leave a brief gap before submitting an identical replacement or allow it to restart once. Reboot persistence: MIG instances never survive a host reboot on any generation, and MIG mode persists across reboots on Ampere (InfoROM) but resets to disabled on Hopper and newer. Provider NVLink health checks: Some managed cloud agents cordon/reboot Nodes when MIG drops GPUs out of full NVLink pair checks; inspect provider node conditions if a MIG Node reboots. See also — Accelerator Requests (keys and request rules) · Hygon MIG Operations (node-wide MIG on Hygon DCUs) · T-Head MIG Operations (MIG partitioning on T-Head PPUs) · Preflight Checks (bare-host MIG checks)

title: NVIDIA MIG Operations

content:
Preflight Checks Run device-manager preflight on a bare host to verify accelerator detection, slicing isolation, RDMA link health, and kubelet TopologyManager configuration before joining a cluster. It drives each vendor’s production allocator directly without needing CRDs, NFD labels, or a running cluster.
Unlike read-only detect and monitor, preflight stages preload libraries and briefly toggles off-state sharing flags when required. It also launches non-privileged probe containers unless --dry-run is passed.
Contents Prerequisites Preflight commands Configuration Probe side effects Checks by manufacturer Result format Prerequisites Run preflight before scheduling live workloads on the host (or pass --dry-run for a zero-write plan):
Temporary occupancy: Probe containers hold each sliceable accelerator briefly while measuring quota enforcement. Staged libraries: Copies /var/lib/gpustack/operator/lib/<manufacturer> onto the host; if the node already runs Device Manager, use the exact same operator image tag so staged preload libraries match. Driver mode toggle: On Ascend (container-share) and Cambricon (smlu-mode), if the sharing flag is off, preflight enables it to confirm driver support and immediately restores it (reporting loudly if restore fails). Probe containers run unprivileged, receiving only the device nodes, mounts, and environment the production allocator injects (--privileged on the outer preflight container covers driver reads and /dev discovery).
Preflight commands Run the command for your hardware vendor. On containerd, replace docker run with nerdctl run (except on Moore Threads and NVIDIA, noted below). Verify each host driver path exists first, because docker run -v creates missing host directories empty and causes detection to report 0 cards.
AMD bashCopy docker run --rm --privileged --network=host \ -v /:/host -v /dev:/dev -v /sys:/sys \ -v /opt/rocm:/opt/rocm:ro -v /opt/rocm/lib:/opt/rocm/lib:ro \ gpustack/gpustack-operator:<tag> \ gpustack-operator device-manager preflight --manufacturer=amd Mount both /opt/rocm and /opt/rocm/lib so the host resolves ROCm symlinks on multi-version installations (or mount -v /opt/rocm/core-<ver>:/opt/rocm:ro to test one version).
Ascend bashCopy docker run --rm --privileged --network=host \ -v /:/host -v /dev:/dev -v /sys:/sys \ -v /usr/local/Ascend:/usr/local/Ascend:ro -v /usr/local/dcmi:/usr/local/dcmi:ro \ gpustack/gpustack-operator:<tag> \ gpustack-operator device-manager preflight --manufacturer=ascend The outer container needs no --runtime ascend because /dev is already mounted; inner Ascend probe containers pass --runtime ascend automatically under docker (and emit commands under nerdctl).
Cambricon bashCopy docker run --rm --privileged --network=host \ -v /:/host -v /dev:/dev -v /sys:/sys \ -v /usr/local/neuware:/usr/local/neuware:ro \ gpustack/gpustack-operator:<tag> \ gpustack-operator device-manager preflight --manufacturer=cambricon Hygon bashCopy docker run --rm --privileged --network=host \ -v /:/host -v /dev:/dev -v /sys:/sys \ -v /opt/hyhal:/opt/hyhal:ro -v /opt/dtk:/opt/dtk:ro \ -v /etc/dmi_mig_config:/etc/dmi_mig_config \ gpustack/gpustack-operator:<tag> \ gpustack-operator device-manager preflight --manufacturer=hygon --probe-image=<image> /etc/dmi_mig_config is mounted writable for MIG registry operations, and --probe-image is required to measure slice checks (Container probes ).
Iluvatar bashCopy docker run --rm --privileged --network=host \ -v /:/host -v /dev:/dev -v /sys:/sys \ -v /usr/local/corex:/usr/local/corex:ro \ gpustack/gpustack-operator:<tag> \ gpustack-operator device-manager preflight --manufacturer=iluvatar MetaX bashCopy docker run --rm --privileged --network=host \ -v /:/host -v /dev:/dev -v /sys:/sys \ -v /opt/mxdriver:/opt/mxdriver:ro -v /opt/maca:/opt/maca:ro \ gpustack/gpustack-operator:<tag> \ gpustack-operator device-manager preflight --manufacturer=metax Moore Threads bashCopy docker run --rm --privileged --network=host --runtime mthreads \ -v /:/host -v /dev:/dev -v /sys:/sys \ gpustack/gpustack-operator:<tag> \ gpustack-operator device-manager preflight --manufacturer=mthreads The mthreads container runtime injects user-space libraries (nerdctl --runtime expects an OCI shim name and cannot invoke mthreads directly).
NVIDIA bashCopy docker run --rm --privileged --network=host --runtime nvidia \ -v /:/host -v /dev:/dev -v /sys:/sys \ gpustack/gpustack-operator:<tag> \ gpustack-operator device-manager preflight --manufacturer=nvidia Pass --runtime nvidia on docker or --gpus all on nerdctl (running under runc hides NVML and reports accelerators: 0 with exit code 1).
T-Head bashCopy docker run --rm --privileged --network=host \ -v /:/host -v /dev:/dev -v /sys:/sys \ -v /usr/local/PPU_SDK:/usr/local/PPU_SDK:ro \ gpustack/gpustack-operator:<tag> \ gpustack-operator device-manager preflight --manufacturer=thead --probe-image=<image> Supply --probe-image carrying the workload PPU SDK to measure slice rows.
All manufacturers bashCopy docker run --rm --network=host -v /:/host \ gpustack/gpustack-operator:<tag> \ gpustack-operator device-manager preflight Without vendor mounts, preflight cross-checks host CLIs on NVIDIA, Ascend, and AMD and prints the required vendor mounts for detected hardware.
Device Manager Pod checks Run detect or dry-run preflight inside an installed gpustack-operator-device-manager-<manufacturer> Pod:
bashCopy kubectl exec -n gpustack-system <device-manager-pod> -- gpustack-operator device-manager detect kubectl exec -n gpustack-system <device-manager-pod> -- \ gpustack-operator device-manager preflight --manufacturer=<manufacturer> The DaemonSet Pod omits /:/host, so preflight enters dry-run mode automatically. It runs detection, device-health, and read-only driver checks, emits container commands, and leaves the node untouched.
Configuration Host access Mount Purpose -v /:/host Enters host root via chroot to run the host container and vendor CLIs and stage preload libraries. --network=host Provides host DNS resolution when pulling probe images inside chroot. -v /dev:/dev, -v /sys:/sys Supplies device nodes and sysfs topology for in-process detection and driver reads. Vendor mount or --runtime Loads user-space vendor management libraries into the preflight process. Command flags Flag Effect --manufacturer Comma-separated manufacturers to check (defaults to all). --no-pci-check Skips PCI presence filtering during detection. --dry-run Prints probe steps without writing host files, toggling driver modes, or starting containers. --probe-image Overrides the probe container image (required on Hygon and T-Head, or for air-gapped hosts). --host-root Host root mount path inside the container (default /host). --runtime Overrides CRI auto-detection (docker, nerdctl, or ctr; missing /host/proc requires explicit --runtime). By default, preflight reads the container runtime from kubelet CRI flags or /var/lib/kubelet/{kubeadm-flags.env,config.yaml}. Otherwise it falls back to docker, nerdctl, or ctr.
Probe side effects On measured tiers, preflight runs one 50%-slice probe per card, then two concurrent slices to verify co-tenancy. Containers carry label gpustack.ai/preflight=true (containerd namespace gpustack-preflight) and are swept before and after each run.
Host write Path Lifecycle Preload libraries /var/lib/gpustack/operator/lib/<manufacturer> Kept on disk (matches Device Manager init-container staging). Per-probe configs /var/lib/gpustack/operator/preflight/ Removed at pass completion (isolated from live .../operator/pods state). Process lock /var/lib/gpustack/operator/preflight/lock File stays; kernel flock releases automatically on process exit. Driver sharing flag Ascend / Cambricon driver state Restored immediately within the same pass. Printed probe commands: Container probes skip execution under --dry-run, missing /host, read-only library paths, missing runtimes, ctr, or nerdctl on Ascend. In those cases, preflight prints the full command (emitted) without failing the exit code.
Checks by manufacturer Each accelerator reports only the modes it currently offers (for example, a MIG-enabled GPU reports partition checks and omits logical-slice rows).
Tier Manufacturers Driver check Capability checks Deepest answer Full NVIDIA, Ascend, AMD, T-Head Yes Real container (sidecar-visibility simulated) measured Container probe Hygon No (note explains why) Real container (sidecar-visibility simulated) measured Driver + injection Cambricon, MetaX Yes Allocator injection only simulated Injection only Iluvatar, MThreads No (note explains why) Allocator injection only simulated Injection checks Iluvatar and Moore Threads enforce slicing in the kernel module and container runtime rather than a user-space flag. preflight verifies allocator injection (simulated) and records an explanatory note.
Container probes Hygon runs real probe containers (measured) with --probe-image (any glibc image carrying sh, cat, grep, awk, mkdir, sleep, and kill). The probe runs /opt/dtk BandwidthTest and reads kfd vgpu sysfs because hy-smi always prints full physical VRAM.
Supported vendor checks Manufacturer Detection API Host cross-check Driver check Target mode Container probe NVIDIA NVML nvidia-smi -L mig-partitioning partitioned Yes Ascend DCMI npu-smi info -l container-share sliced Yes AMD RSMI, AMDSMI, HSA rocm-smi --showuniqueid cu-mask-topology sliced Yes T-Head HGML — mig-partitioning partitioned Yes Cambricon CNDev — smlu-mode sliced — MetaX MXSML, sGPU sysfs — sgpu-mode sliced — Hygon RSMI, AMDGPU, HSA — — sliced / partitioned Yes Iluvatar IXML — — sliced — MThreads MTML — — sliced — Compare vendors by the report’s mode field rather than vendor-specific capability names.
Driver checks Check ok meaning not-declared meaning unavailable meaning mig-partitioning Physical partition profile declared MIG off or unsupported on card Driver query failed container-share Flag on, or toggled on and restored Generation has no flag DCMI missing or refused cu-mask-topology HSA topology and CU atom validated — HSA init failed or card missing smlu-mode Mode on, or toggled on and restored Card advertises no sMLU capacity CNDev missing sMLU API or refused sgpu-mode sGPU sysfs registry readable — Registry unreadable Ascend A5 host checks On Atlas A5 (950) NPUs, preflight adds two node-level declared checks on every card:
Check Reads ok meaning unavailable meaning ascend-docker-runtime /usr/local/Ascend version MindCluster 26.0.0+ Older or unreadable runtime hccl-ranktable /host/etc/hccl_rootinfo.json Absent or JSON version 2.0 Wrong version, symlink, invalid JSON, or missing /host See Vendor Prerequisites for remediation.
Slice probes Each slice probe requests 50% of one card (so a 24564 MiB card reports 12282 MiB inside the probe):
Manufacturer Default probe image Vendor runtime Probe reader Cap source NVIDIA nvidia/cuda:<CUDA major> --runtime nvidia / --gpus all nvidia-smi --query-gpu=memory.total CUDA_DEVICE_MEMORY_LIMIT_<i> Ascend quay.io/ascend/cann:<CANN major>-<family> --runtime ascend (docker) enpu-monitor npu_info.config (memory-quota) AMD ubuntu:24.04 None rocm-monitor VROCM_DEVICE_MEMORY_LIMIT_<i> T-Head Required via --probe-image None ppu-monitor HGGC_DEVICE_MEMORY_LIMIT_<i> Hygon Required via --probe-image None BandwidthTest + kfd vgpu sysfs vdev0.conf (mem) Capability rows report sliced-runtime-loaded (shim or vgpu active), sliced-quota-in-force (50% VRAM cap), sidecar-visibility (simulated SSH grant), and co-tenancy (two slices on one card).
Result format preflight writes one YAML report to stdout with accelerators, network (NIC record inspection ), and topology (configured kubelet topologyManagerPolicy, or unknown when unset):
yamlCopy accelerators: - manufacturer: nvidia detection: state: ok depth: declared accelerators: 8 checks: [] network: timestamp: "2026-10-29T00:00:00Z" checks: [] topology: timestamp: "2026-10-29T00:00:00Z" policy: single-numa-node depth: declared Check states and depth State Meaning Exit code ok Capability verified at reported depth (declared, simulated, or measured) 0 not-declared Hardware does not offer this capability 0 unavailable Offered capability, detection, lock, crash guard, or stale sweep failed Non-zero Broken RDMA links and topology: unknown or none do not fail the exit code because accelerator allocation still works. Concurrent runs fail closed on /var/lib/gpustack/operator/preflight/lock, vendor panics report preflight-panicked, and failed sweeps report stale-container-sweep (clean via gpustack.ai/preflight=true or gpustack-preflight).
Unhealthy accelerators Uncorrectable ECC or hardware faults (status.unhealthy: true) keep detection ok (NVIDIA A100 x8 (1 unhealthy)) while healthy cards run full checks. Each faulty card emits capability: device-health (state: unavailable, non-zero exit) because the device plugin withholds unhealthy cards.
See also — Vendor Prerequisites (host drivers and runtimes per vendor) · Accelerator Requests (resource keys and admission rules) · RDMA Operations (kubelet TopologyManager setup and NIC inspection)
