All 18 rounds finished with zero failed requests, verified UID-preconditioned cleanup and return to 1 replica.
Checkpoints (B1–C3) record phase progress, while scale-up elapsed times track wall clock from ramp start (in-flight drain and harness transitions extend actual wall time past the nominal 45 s ramp + 45 s sustain windows).
Starting from one replica on H200, unmargined TokenThroughput manual arms stayed at 1 replica (~14.5k tok/s at c = 24 sat below 17135.159 tok/s). TokenThroughput catalog triggered at R2, and after ~76 s of vLLM startup became Ready at S3 (99.6–105.6 s from ramp start), costing +33.7% median readyReplicaSeconds (317.04 versus 237.094 s) with no sustain TTFT win (343.842 versus 321.352 ms).
Predictive triggered earlier (15.1–21.9 s from ramp start) and reached Ready by checkpoint R3 (81.9–94.6 s elapsed from ramp start), cutting sustain TTFT p50 to 189.511 ms (catalog), 194.733 ms (frozen-manual) and 206.453 ms (tuned-manual).
Latency columns show p50 / p99:
Algorithm Arm Valid repeats Ready replica-s (median/min–max) Peak Ready Ramp TTFT (ms) Sustain TTFT (ms) Sustain ITL (ms) TokenThroughput frozen-manual 3 / 3 237.239 (232.445–309.809) 1 350.355 / 551.351 319.235 / 529.512 6.349 / 9.931 TokenThroughput tuned-manual 3 / 3 237.094 (234.374–304.551) 1 348.907 / 548.91 321.352 / 517.771 6.345 / 9.776 TokenThroughput catalog 3 / 3 317.04 (289.786–331.45) 2 350.432 / 553.104 343.842 / 522.326 6.346 / 9.365 Predictive frozen-manual 3 / 3 393.755 (366.408–396.625) 2 336.061 / 549.38 194.733 / 315.066 5.797 / 7.679 Predictive tuned-manual 3 / 3 392.089 (370.123–392.919) 2 350.769 / 564.252 206.453 / 370.607 5.744 / 8.301 Predictive catalog 3 / 3 423.031 (392.662–679.002) 2 349.685 / 554.122 189.511 / 364.141 5.741 / 9.839 Algorithm sensitivity A 360-second H200 hardware wave (baseline 60 s c = 2, ramp 90 s c = 24, sustain 90 s c = 24, cooldown 120 s c = 0, maxReplicas: 4) compared Proportional (RunningRequests target 8), TokenThroughput (14000 tok/s) and catalog-backed Predictive (12851.37 tok/s) using True SLO (TTFT <= 2000 ms and adjacent ITL <= 33 ms) and Goodput.
Those metric definitions match the deterministic synthetic simulation (model output, not GPU hardware), where Predictive reached 99.4% true SLO on a five-step synthetic ramp seed against 76.1% for reactive configurations.
On the H200 hardware wave, catalog-backed Predictive reached 3 Ready replicas by R2 and 4 by R3, cutting ramp TTFT p50 from 347.282–350.591 ms to 192.093 ms and sustain TTFT p50 to 120.59 ms (3886.136 output tok/s, zero failed requests). Exception: TokenThroughput recorded 11 failed requests out of 1,272 in sustain (True SLO 0.9914), while Proportional and Predictive kept 1.0 with zero failures.
Algorithm Phase Requests Failed True SLO Goodput (req/s) TTFT p50 / p90 / p99 (ms) ITL p50 / p90 / p99 (ms) Output (tok/s) Proportional baseline 88 0 1.0 1.447 49.439 / 50.846 / 75.688 5.217 / 5.346 / 5.61 370.386 Proportional ramp 1008 0 1.0 11.045 347.282 / 527.093 / 545.355 6.349 / 6.681 / 11.18 2827.554 Proportional sustain 1244 0 1.0 13.618 190.555 / 325.042 / 338.779 5.75 / 6.008 / 7.864 3486.167 TokenThroughput baseline 88 0 1.0 1.448 49.263 / 51.251 / 76.935 5.213 / 5.339 / 5.606 370.565 TokenThroughput ramp 1008 0 1.0 11.041 350.591 / 527.408 / 551.491 6.345 / 6.693 / 10.942 2826.369 TokenThroughput sustain 1272 11 0.9914 13.807 145.939 / 171.786 / 262.921 5.795 / 6.025 / 12.969 3534.61 Predictive baseline 88 0 1.0 1.447 49.742 / 51.305 / 76.375 5.214 / 5.344 / 5.598 370.495 Predictive ramp 1244 0 1.0 13.625 192.093 / 325.727 / 340.679 5.746 / 6.004 / 7.8 3487.99 Predictive sustain 1383 0 1.0 15.18 120.59 / 187.599 / 195.3 5.596 / 5.847 / 7.21 3886.136 Embedded catalog An openai/gpt-oss-120b (fp4, vllm, 1 × H200) Server deployment ran with capacityPrior: {} and no catalogRef or identity annotations against the embedded catalog. It inferred Server/openai/gpt-oss-120b/fp4/vllm/nvidia-h200/gpus=1,tp=1,ep=1,pp=1,dp=1,ldp=1,cp=1 (profileDigest: sha256:47d96f0e...), resolved seedTokensPerSecond: "6405.44" (ExplicitSaturation, P95 TTFT 2000 ms, ITL 33 ms) and set effectiveTokensPerSecond: "4804.08".
A 60-second concurrency-8 check completed 176 requests with zero errors at 4862.388 total tok/s (915.002 output tok/s; TTFT p50 / p90 / p95 96.185 / 225.437 / 238.947 ms; ITL p50 / p90 / p95 10.958 / 11.713 / 12.014 ms), within 1.2% of the embedded effective prior.
H200 serving comparison Re-running the five disaggregated configurations across four single-GPU H200 nodes (Qwen3-8B for PD; Qwen3-VL-8B-Instruct in 1R1E2P1D for EPD) yielded:
Configuration Phase Requests Errors TTFT p50 / p99 (ms) ITL p50 / p99 (ms) Output (tok/s) vllm-pd-proportional ramp / sustain 405 / 396 0 / 0 2302.954 / 3049.929 (p99: 4451.863 / 3960.101) 8.443 / 8.305 (p99: 17.251 / 16.239) 1317.793 / 1277.5 vllm-pd-token-throughput ramp / sustain 106047 / 379 105965 / 0 2893.8 / 3009.197 (p99: 5559.696 / 4658.621) 8.073 / 8.122 (p99: 15.248 / 15.483) 279.875 / 1227.049 vllm-pd-predictive ramp / sustain 107447 / 364 107367 / 0 2719.156 / 3146.237 (p99: 30051.934 / 6013.353) 8.282 / 8.309 (p99: 16.401 / 16.66) 273.052 / 1177.547 sglang-pd-token-throughput ramp / sustain 1245 / 2904 906 / 2904 2203.669 / - (p99: 3620.957 / -) 5.723 / - (p99: 22.806 / -) 1151.088 / 0 vllm-epd-predictive ramp / sustain 180 / 180 0 / 0 943.066 / 1044.397 (p99: 3678.427 / 3493.704) 8.285 / 8.215 (p99: 15.968 / 16.934) 1617.037 / 1475.286 vllm-pd-proportional scaled decode (1 → 2, lead 24 s) and vllm-epd-predictive scaled prefill (1 → 2) with zero errors across all four phases. When vllm-pd-token-throughput and vllm-pd-predictive added a second prefill replica during high-rate text ramp, the Router returned fast HTTP 503s until registration finished, then served sustain and cooldown with zero errors.
Verification Scale-out timing Scale-out lead measures ramp start to the first sampled desired count above 1 (not Ready time). A count already above 1 at ramp start reports 0 with Pre-ramp count >1 set to Yes.
Configuration Lead (s) Pre-ramp count >1 Maximum desired counts Maximum Ready counts vllm-pd-proportional (H100) 30 No Prefill 2, decode 2 Prefill 2, decode 2 vllm-pd-token-throughput (H100) 0 Yes Prefill 2, decode 2 Prefill 2, decode 2 vllm-pd-predictive (H100) 0 Yes Prefill 2, decode 2 Prefill 2, decode 2 sglang-pd-token-throughput (H100) 0 Yes Prefill 2, decode 2 Prefill 2, decode 2 vllm-epd-predictive (H100) 0 Yes Encode 1, prefill 2, decode 2 Encode 1, prefill 2, decode 2 Server TokenThroughput catalog (H200) 22–28 No Server 2 Server 2 Server Predictive catalog (H200) 15–22 No Server 2 Server 2 In Suite 2, every single-Server run started ramp at 1 Ready replica: Predictive committed growth at 15.1–21.9 s versus 22.2–28.2 s for TokenThroughput catalog.
Retirement The standalone single-role lifecycle check verified scale-out, serving at two replicas, Disqualified and Draining during scale-down, and serving on one survivor:
Lifecycle phase Requests Errors Observation Scale-out (up) 13073 7 Router returned HTTP 503 with connection termination Two replicas (two) 14810 0 Expanded deployment served requests Scale-down (down) 1880 0 Retirement observed while traffic continued One replica (one) 942 0 One Ready survivor served requests The earlier Wave 2 check also recorded 3 failures in 10,579 scale-out requests. Admission passed all 45 checks; the standalone lifecycle check passed 10 checks and failed its all-phases check.
Suite 1 timelines sampled Disqualified on proportional and token-based PD (plus Admitted and Aborted on predictive PD) and no retirement state on EPD. The retirement protocol transitions Draining → Deleting (distinct from Kubernetes Terminating). Before trusting live recommendations, verify partial: false and missing[] via /metrics (Engine signals ).
Additional runtime-acceptance runs verified:
vLLM multi-Server manual scaling (1 → 2 → 1): Router worker set followed every edit, round_robin split 16 requests 8/8 at two replicas, and 21/21 checks passed. vLLM External DP retirement (DP = 2): Router held 2 → 4 → 2 workers; withdrawal reached the Router in 21 s and retired members deleted at 70 s (honoring the 60 s handoff window). Eight checks passed; one check failed from timing withdrawal against the 60 s window (case bug). SGLang PD active scaling: 29/29 checks passed; Mooncake moved 54 MB across six direct transfers with zero failures; the scaler read 24 waiting requests on decode, scaled decode to 2, and returned both roles to 1. Suite 2 single-Server rounds: All 12 rounds that scaled to 2 (3 TokenThroughput catalog and 9 Predictive) returned to 1 Ready replica with zero failed requests. Limitations Suite 1 (one 8-H100 node) and Suite 2 (four 1-H200 nodes) do not establish a universal algorithm ranking or optimal headroom margin across workloads. Text and multimodal clients run different work and stopping rules, so throughput values are not comparable across modes. Image tags do not prove identical internal engine packages. Zero errors apply only to those measured requests: multi-node H200 PD prefill scale-out hit transient Router 503s during registration, and SGLang PD reproduced Mooncake KV transfer errors. See Scaling Walkthrough for the boundary between configuration examples and captured lifecycle evidence. title: Model Deployment Scaling Benchmark

content:
Model Deployment Scaling A ModelDeploymentScaler computes target replica counts for one ModelDeployment from live engine metrics and publishes recommendations in status. In Active mode, it writes spec.roles[].replicas on the target so the ModelDeployment controller scales and retires instances.
Contents Configuration Algorithms Scaling policy Replica ownership Status Limitations Troubleshooting Configuration yamlCopy apiVersion: worker.gpustack.ai/v1 kind: ModelDeploymentScaler # namespaced, short name mds metadata: name: llm-serving namespace: team-a spec: targetRef: name: llm-serving # required, immutable; ModelDeployment in this namespace mode: Shadow # default; enum: Shadow, Active suspend: false # default; true stops planning and releases binding sampling: intervalSeconds: 15 # default; range 5..300 pendingTimeoutSeconds: 300 # default; range 60..1200 roles: # required; include every target role - name: server minReplicas: 2 # optional, default: 1; range 1..1024 (no scale-to-zero) maxReplicas: 16 # required; range 1..1024, >= minReplicas algorithm: # one type and its matching parameter block only type: Proportional proportional: metric: QueueDepth # required; running + waiting requests tolerance: "0.1" # optional, default: 0.1; range (0, 1] roleTargets: - name: server target: "8" # required positive quantity; requests per ready replica behavior: scaleUp: stabilizationWindowSeconds: 0 # default; range 0..600 maxStepReplicas: 4 # default; 0 or omitted stores 4 maxStepPercent: 100 # default; 0 or omitted stores 100 # Optional: replace both bounds with one unit; value 0 disables scale-up. # stepPolicy: # type: Pods # enum: Pods, Percent # value: 2 # required, nonnegative scaleDown: stabilizationWindowSeconds: 300 # default; range 0..1800 cooldownAfterAbortSeconds: 300 # default; range 0..3600 decodePostScaleUpGraceSeconds: 120 # default; range 0..3600, Decode only # Optional: replace default 1 replica per pass; value 0 disables scale-down. # stepPolicy: # type: Percent # enum: Pods, Percent # value: 10 # required, nonnegative rebalance: policy: Opposing # default; enum: Opposing, Priority, Disabled Target ordering: A scaler may be created before its target; it reports TargetNotFound until the ModelDeployment exists. Mode and suspend: Shadow plans without claiming ownership; Active acquires the Scaler ownership rules and commits counts. suspend: true pauses planning and releases ownership. Quick check: Run kubectl get mds to read mode, algorithm and Bound, Active and Blocked conditions. Algorithms algorithm.type selects Proportional, TokenThroughput or Predictive (inferred from a present proportional or predictive block; otherwise defaults to TokenThroughput).
In a deterministic synthetic simulation (model output, not a hardware run) on identical open-loop seeds, Predictive reached 99.4% true SLO compliance on ramp versus 76.1% for reactive algorithms, and quota-shortfall verified pendingTimeoutSeconds rollback.
Online Auto calibration remains deferred. See Scaling Benchmark for live H100 and H200 measurements and Step 3: Choose an algorithm .
Algorithm Mechanism Best fit Main constraint Proportional Instantaneous metric over fixed per-replica target with tolerance deadband Uniform-length requests Bursts and shifting lengths skew fixed targets TokenThroughput Default. Stable and panic sliding windows over cache-adjusted token rates plus p95 TTFT/ITL guards General LLM and PD workloads with prefix caching Reacts after demand changes Predictive Causal Kalman filter forecasting horizonSeconds ahead, floored by TokenThroughput Sustained ramps where pre-warming offsets startup latency Falls back to TokenThroughput until minPoints arrive Proportional Recommends ceil(total / target) (minimum 1) when observed load per ready replica leaves the tolerance band. metric accepts QueueDepth, RunningRequests, WaitingRequests, PromptTokensPerSecond, GenerationTokensPerSecond or TotalTokensPerSecond. Every scaled role needs a target or a direct ratio to a targeted role.
Token throughput yamlCopy apiVersion: worker.gpustack.ai/v1 kind: ModelDeploymentScaler metadata: name: llm-serving namespace: team-a spec: targetRef: name: llm-serving mode: Active roles: - name: encode minReplicas: 1 maxReplicas: 4 - name: prefill minReplicas: 2 maxReplicas: 16 - name: decode minReplicas: 2 maxReplicas: 16 ratios: - numeratorRole: prefill denominatorRole: decode target: "1" min: "0.5" max: "2" - numeratorRole: encode denominatorRole: prefill target: "0.5" algorithm: type: TokenThroughput tokenThroughput: prefillTargetTokensPerSecond: "2000" # prompt capacity per Prefill replica decodeTargetTokensPerSecond: "800" # generation capacity per Decode replica # serverTargetTokensPerSecond: "2000" # combined capacity for Server role stableWindowSeconds: 180 # default; range 30..600 panicWindowSeconds: 60 # default; range 10..300, < stableWindowSeconds panicThreshold: "2" # default; positive quantity ttftTargetMilliseconds: "500" # default; positive quantity itlTargetMilliseconds: "50" # default; positive quantity latencyQuantile: "0.95" # default; P95 Role capacity: Supply prompt rate for Prefill, generation rate for Decode, combined rate for Server; couple Encode through a ratio. Panic and latency guards: Demand at panicThreshold × ready capacity enters panic and blocks scale-down. A time to first token (TTFT) or inter-token latency (ITL) breach holds scale-down; above 1.2× target triggers growth. Predictive Forecasts token demand horizonSeconds ahead via a Kalman filter, floored by nested tokenThroughput:
yamlCopy apiVersion: worker.gpustack.ai/v1 kind: ModelDeploymentScaler metadata: name: llm-serving namespace: team-a spec: targetRef: name: llm-serving mode: Active roles: - name: prefill minReplicas: 2 maxReplicas: 16 - name: decode minReplicas: 2 maxReplicas: 16 algorithm: type: Predictive predictive: tokenThroughput: prefillTargetTokensPerSecond: "2000" decodeTargetTokensPerSecond: "800" horizonSeconds: 300 # default; range 30..600 prefillTokenCapacityPerReplica: "2000" decodeTokenCapacityPerReplica: "800" # serverTokenCapacityPerReplica: "2000" qLevel: "1" # default level process noise qTrend: "0.1" # default trend process noise measurementNoise: "10" # default observation noise minPoints: 6 # default; range 1..64 Before minPoints arrive (PredictorWarmingUp), Predictive uses the TokenThroughput fallback. After warm-up, panic or latency above 1.2× target adds at least one replica, and scale-down requires survivors to stay at or below 80% capacity.
Engine signals Both engines report running and waiting queues (SGLang adds sglang:num_decode_transfer_queue_reqs and sglang:num_prefill_inflight_queue_reqs). Prompt rate adjusts for prefix-cache hits; generation rate reads rank-0 deltas; latency reads histogram quantiles with no mean fallback if buckets hit +Inf.
Inspect live samples, partial scrapes and missing series through the ModelDeployment /metrics subresource (requires RBAC get on modeldeployments/metrics):
bashCopy kubectl get --raw "/apis/worker.gpustack.ai/v1/namespaces/<namespace>/modeldeployments/<name>/metrics" \ | jq '{partial, missing, processing, queueing, latency}' The subresource scrapes up to 64 owned Pods (prometheus.io/scrape: "true", prometheus.io/port, prometheus.io/scheme; take-over roles[].command roles omit scrape annotations) and returns 503 Service Unavailable when no owned Pod answers.
partial: true: Marks unreadable or TLS-untrusted endpoints, first counter reads, counter resets, missing TTFT histograms or > 64 Pods. missing[] with partial: false: Normal for zero-count error counters, idle windows or unconfigured cache tiers. Capacity priors spec.algorithm.capacityPrior fills omitted token capacities for TokenThroughput and Predictive (Proportional rejects it) from an offline catalog (embedded priors.yaml or a same-namespace ConfigMap). Missing or incompatible profiles fail closed (CapacityPriorUnresolved, InsufficientLoadCoverage, IncompatibleMetric).
yamlCopy apiVersion: worker.gpustack.ai/v1 kind: ModelDeploymentScaler metadata: name: qwen-scaler namespace: team-a spec: targetRef: name: llm-serving roles: - name: prefill maxReplicas: 8 - name: decode maxReplicas: 8 algorithm: type: TokenThroughput # also supported on Predictive tokenThroughput: latencyQuantile: "0.90" # resolve prior at P90 instead of P95 ttftTargetMilliseconds: "2000" # required explicitly for catalog Prefill/Server itlTargetMilliseconds: "33" # required explicitly for catalog Decode/Server capacityPrior: catalogRef: # optional; omit for embedded catalog (no fallback when set) name: capacity-priors # same-namespace ConfigMap key: priors.yaml # default (falls back to priors.json) headroom: "0.75" # default in (0, 1]; multiplies catalog seed only Explicit latency targets: Required when using the catalog (TTFT for Prefill, ITL for Decode, both for Server); default 500 ms / 50 ms values are suppressed. Disaggregated ratios: PD and EPD catalog resolution requires fixed connected ratios (min == max) across all roles; partial manual overrides are refused. Admission behavior: CREATE rejects unresolved priors when the target exists (warns if absent for GitOps ordering); UPDATE warns so you can suspend, switch to Shadow or fix fields. See Suite 2: Capacity priors and Resolving a catalog prior . Catalog matching requirements The resolver infers model, hardware and precision from spec.model (ModelArtifact), AcceleratorType and --quantization. Pin or cross-check identities with optional ModelDeployment annotations:
Annotation Purpose worker.gpustack.ai/model-id Model identity guard (natural name or normalized alias) worker.gpustack.ai/hardware-id Hardware identity guard (accelerator name or slug) worker.gpustack.ai/prefill-hardware-id Prefill hardware guard for heterogeneous targets worker.gpustack.ai/decode-hardware-id Decode hardware guard for heterogeneous targets worker.gpustack.ai/precision Precision selector (fp8, bf16, fp4, etc.) Catalog resolution supports single-Pod managed Server, PD and EPD roles with whole-card resources (no slicing, Elastic EP, External DP, spec.kvCache or roles[].command).
Scaling policy Replica bounds and ratios roles[] defines minReplicas and maxReplicas for every target role. ratios[] couples distinct roles with min, max and preferred target (equal values fix a ratio). The planner projects recommendations onto one feasible vector; if current replicas violate bounds or ratios, planning stops (BoundsConflict or RatioConflict) until the policy includes them.
Scaling rates and safeguards Scale-up step: Without stepPolicy, each pass adds up to max(maxStepReplicas, ceil(current * maxStepPercent)). Set stepPolicy (type: Pods or type: Percent; value: 0 blocks movement) to enforce one bound. Scale-down step and holds: Defaults to 1 replica per pass without stepPolicy. Scale-down holds when any role lacks ready replicas or full metrics, during panic/missing signals, during active retirement or abort cooldown, or during Decode post-scale-up grace. Pending timeout and abort rollback: Unadmitted scale-up cohorts hold growth and revert to baseline after pendingTimeoutSeconds (ResourceExhausted). An Aborted retirement restores pre-scale-down counts (ScaleDownAborted), cancels rebalance and starts cooldownAfterAbortSeconds. Retirement versus pause: Unlike roles[].pause: true (holds Pods and quota under RolePaused), retirement withdraws endpoint-eligible (30 s), drains (240 s, after 60 s disaggregated handoff grace) and deletes Pods and Workload (30 s; 300 s total). Re-declaring the ordinal before Deleting cancels retirement (RetirementAdopted); see Pause and retirement . Resource rebalancing When a scale-up times out and reverts while the receiver still needs capacity, rebalance.policy decides whether a donor on the same nonempty acceleratorType retires one replica first:
Policy Donor rule Opposing Default. Donor’s own recommendation must be to shrink. Priority Lower-priority role in rebalance.priority[] may donate while holding. Disabled No donation attempted. yamlCopy apiVersion: worker.gpustack.ai/v1 kind: ModelDeploymentScaler metadata: name: qwen-scaler namespace: team-a spec: targetRef: name: llm-serving roles: - name: prefill maxReplicas: 8 - name: decode maxReplicas: 8 - name: encode maxReplicas: 4 algorithm: type: Proportional proportional: metric: WaitingRequests roleTargets: - name: prefill target: "8" - name: decode target: "8" - name: encode target: "4" rebalance: policy: Priority priority: # highest first; unlisted roles neither donate nor receive - decode - prefill - encode RebalanceNotApplicable means no donor shares the pool; RebalanceBlocked means an intermediate vector violates policy or a Priority donation already ran in this exhaustion episode.
Replica ownership Scaler ownership rules An Active scaler claims target replicas with two annotations on the ModelDeployment:
Annotation Payload modeldeployment.gpustack.ai/scaler-binding scalerName, scalerUID and monotonic term modeldeployment.gpustack.ai/scaler-decision decisionID, term and committed vector Admission rejects user edits to replica counts or either annotation on a bound target while allowing other edits. A competing scaler reports AlreadyBound; target recreation reports TargetReplaced until acknowledged by a scaler edit; corrupt annotations report InvalidBinding. To clear an orphaned binding after scaler deletion, remove the annotation without editing replica counts.
GitOps sync Ignore each role’s replicas and both scaler annotations (~1 escapes /) in GitOps tools:
yamlCopy apiVersion: argoproj.io/v1alpha1 kind: Application metadata: name: llm-serving namespace: argocd spec: ignoreDifferences: - group: worker.gpustack.ai kind: ModelDeployment name: llm-serving namespace: default jsonPointers: - /spec/roles/0/replicas - /metadata/annotations/modeldeployment.gpustack.ai~1scaler-binding - /metadata/annotations/modeldeployment.gpustack.ai~1scaler-decision syncPolicy: syncOptions: - RespectIgnoreDifferences=true Flux Kustomization uses the same paths under spec.ignore[].paths:
yamlCopy apiVersion: kustomize.toolkit.fluxcd.io/v1 kind: Kustomization metadata: name: gpustack-operator namespace: flux-system spec: ignore: - target: group: worker.gpustack.ai kind: ModelDeployment name: llm-serving namespace: default paths: - /spec/roles/0/replicas - /metadata/annotations/modeldeployment.gpustack.ai~1scaler-binding - /metadata/annotations/modeldeployment.gpustack.ai~1scaler-decision Status Compare status.roles[].rawRecommendedReplicas against constrainedReplicas and reason (WithinTolerance, Panic, NoReadyReplicas, LatencyGuardHold, LatencyGuardScaleUp, PredictorWarmingUp, PredictiveConsolidationHold, RatioCoupled). signalState reports Fresh, Idle, Missing or Stale.
Condition Success reason Other reasons Bound Bound TargetNotFound, AlreadyBound, TargetReplaced, InvalidBinding, Suspended Active Active TargetNotFound, AlreadyBound, TargetReplaced, InvalidBinding, Suspended, ShadowMode, CapacityPriorUnresolved, InsufficientLoadCoverage, IncompatibleMetric MetricsReady Observed WaitingForMetrics, ResourceExhausted, BoundsConflict, RatioConflict CapacityPriorsReady Resolved, Disabled CapacityPriorUnresolved, InsufficientLoadCoverage, IncompatibleMetric, TargetNotFound, TargetReplaced, InvalidBinding, Suspended Blocked Ready (False) BoundsConflict, RatioConflict, PacingBounded, ResourceExhausted, ScaleDownAborted, RebalanceNotApplicable, RebalanceBlocked, CapacityPriorUnresolved, InsufficientLoadCoverage, IncompatibleMetric, RolePaused RolePaused holds replica writes while a target role is paused (Scaling during pause ). Check observedGeneration, lastCommit, pendingCohort, rebalance, lastScaleDown and resolvedCapacityPriors.
Limitations Admission rejects roles using roles[].command or elastic.dataParallelWidth, and requires generated group names at maxReplicas to fit Kubernetes’s 63-character label limit. The sampler scrapes at most 64 ready Pods per role (incomplete coverage holds scale-down), and rate/latency windows need at least two valid samples. Deployments without spec.router cannot prove direct Service withdrawal and abort retirement at 30 s. On SGLang PD, set terminationGracePeriodSeconds: 45. Both webhooks use failurePolicy: Fail; a webhook outage rejects fenced writes while existing replicas keep serving. Troubleshooting Symptom Signal Owner & action Counts never change Active=False (ShadowMode, Suspended, TargetNotFound, AlreadyBound, TargetReplaced) On the ModelDeploymentScaler, set mode: Active, clear suspend, or resolve the duplicate/replaced target binding. Counts never change MetricsReady=False (WaitingForMetrics), signalState: Missing/Stale Query the ModelDeployment /metrics subresource (jq '{partial,missing}'), repair unreadable Pods and wait two intervals. Counts never change CapacityPriorsReady=False Fix catalogRef ConfigMap, target identity annotations, single-Pod topology and explicit latency targets, or supply explicit capacities on the scaler. Counts never change Blocked=True (BoundsConflict, RatioConflict, RolePaused, PacingBounded) Adjust scaler bounds/ratios, clear roles[].pause on the ModelDeployment, or wait for pacing/retirement windows. Counts revert after growth pendingCohort, ResourceExhausted Inspect Kueue ClusterQueue quota and Workload status on the target’s pool before retrying growth. Counts revert after shrinking lastScaleDown (Aborted), target status.retirement Inspect kubectl -n <ns> get md <name> -o json | jq '.status.retirement': add spec.router if aborted at 30 s, or fix stuck/busy Pods before cooldown ends. Write refused by webhook Admission error on ModelDeployment Configure GitOps sync ignore paths or clear an orphaned binding annotation after deleting the scaler. See also — Model Deployment Configuration (role fields, readiness and rollout) · Scaling Benchmark (H100 and H200 measurements) · Scaling Walkthrough (configure and observe) · Online Runtime Control (role pause guard and retirement budgets) · Model Deployment Routing (router withdrawal and endpoint eligibility)
Next → Model Deployment Scaling Benchmark — review H100 and H200 scaling measurements.

RDMA Networking Device Manager discovers healthy remote direct memory access (RDMA) endpoints and advertises them as Kubernetes extended resources. Kubelet allocates endpoints to containers that request them.
Contents Overview Configuration Operations Troubleshooting Overview Interface discovery The node inventory records link health in Devices, the device plugin advertises eligible RDMA keys, and kubelet grants endpoints to containers. Kueue queue admission does not meter RDMA keys.
Configuration RDMA requests Select an RDMA key and endpoint count in RDMA resource requests , configure an optional DevicesRDMASelectionPolicy in Selection policy , and inspect link states in NIC record inspection .
Operations Step 1: Inspect capacity Check allocatable device.gpustack.ai/rdma* keys across Nodes.
Step 2: Configure NUMA alignment Configure the kubelet TopologyManager policy when containers require non-uniform memory access (NUMA) alignment (Enabling NUMA alignment ).
Step 3: Verify RDMA allocation Follow the RDMA Networking Walkthrough and confirm the active kubelet policy in Verification .
Troubleshooting Follow Troubleshooting to resolve unhealthy links, missing rdma.capable labels, TopologyAffinityError rejections, or Pods stuck Pending behind exhausted endpoints.
See also — Topology (domain placement) · Heterogeneous Devices (accelerator allocation)
Next → RDMA Operations — select RDMA keys, filter adapters, and align NUMA placement.
title: RDMA Networking

content:
RDMA Operations Select a remote direct memory access (RDMA) resource key, filter host channel adapters (HCAs) with DevicesRDMASelectionPolicy, align kubelet non-uniform memory access (NUMA) placement, and verify granted devices. See Accelerator Requests for Pod admission rules.
Contents RDMA resource requests Selection policy Enabling NUMA alignment Verification EFA engine images Troubleshooting RDMA resource requests Device Manager advertises three RDMA resource keys depending on each interface’s configuration:
Key Mode Request unit Tokens device.gpustack.ai/rdma Exclusive One whole interface 1 per endpoint device.gpustack.ai/rdma.shared Shared One concurrent share of an interface 64 per endpoint device.gpustack.ai/rdma.partitioned Partitioned One SR-IOV virtual function 1 per virtual function A single-root I/O virtualization (SR-IOV) physical function with virtual functions serves device.gpustack.ai/rdma.partitioned only; all other RDMA interfaces serve rdma and rdma.shared (accounting for allocations independently across the two families). AWS Elastic Fabric Adapter (EFA) devices use the AWS plugin key vpc.amazonaws.com/efa.
Inspect allocatable RDMA keys across the cluster before writing manifests:
bashCopy kubectl get nodes -o json | jq -r '.items[] | .metadata.name as $n | .status.allocatable | with_entries(select(.key | startswith("device.gpustack.ai/rdma"))) | select(length > 0) | {node: $n} + .' Prefer device.gpustack.ai/rdma.shared unless the workload requires exclusive family reservations (hardware queue pairs isolate concurrent processes on one adapter). On managed ModelDeployments, set spec.roles[].resources.interface instead of raw Pod keys (Model Deployment Configuration ); EFA paths also require a custom engine image (EFA engine images ).
Endpoints per accelerator Request one RDMA endpoint per requested accelerator (N accelerators and N endpoints in the same container). Device plugins publish only NUMA-node hints rather than 1:1 PCIe switch pairings, so kubelet TopologyManager controls locality:
none (Kubernetes default): Allocates accelerators and HCAs independently, allowing cross-socket assignments with silent throughput loss. restricted or single-numa-node: Constrains both allocations to matching NUMA node(s), leaving exact HCA-to-GPU pairing inside a NUMA node to the workload. Node labels rdma.distance and rdma.numa are informational node summaries; feature.gpustack.ai/rdma.capable=true gates whether at least one usable RDMA endpoint exists on the Node.
GPU and RDMA requests yamlCopy apiVersion: v1 kind: Pod metadata: name: rdma-trainer namespace: team-a labels: kueue.x-k8s.io/queue-name: <local-queue> # required for accelerator webhook checks spec: nodeSelector: gpu.gpustack.ai/model: b300 # user label identifying verified NIC/GPU hardware layout containers: - name: trainer image: nvcr.io/nvidia/pytorch:24.10-py3 resources: limits: nvidia.com/gpu: "8" # whole accelerators (partition tokens publish no NUMA hint) device.gpustack.ai/rdma: "8" # same container so container-scoped TopologyManager aligns both On device.gpustack.ai/rdma.shared, preferred allocation spreads tokens one per healthy HCA in outer rounds before reusing an HCA, so requesting N shared units across N healthy HCAs assigns distinct adapters first.
Injected devices Every RDMA allocation (rdma, rdma.shared, or rdma.partitioned) injects deduplicated character devices and HCA environment variables into the container:
Injected item Value /dev/infiniband/uverbs<N> One character device per distinct granted HCA (allocation fails whole if any node is missing). /dev/infiniband/rdma_cm At most one connection-manager device per allocation response, when present on the host. NCCL_IB_HCA Sorted, comma-joined HCA names prefixed with = (such as =mlx5_1,mlx5_10, or =mlx5_1:1,mlx5_10:1 when a selection policy pins port). GPUSTACK_RDMA_DEVICES Sorted, comma-joined bare HCA names without = or port suffixes (mlx5_1,mlx5_10). bashCopy ls /dev/infiniband echo "$NCCL_IB_HCA" echo "$GPUSTACK_RDMA_DEVICES" Policy exclusion after grant: If an active DevicesRDMASelectionPolicy later excludes all endpoints of a new grant, the response injects empty NCCL_IB_HCA="" and GPUSTACK_RDMA_DEVICES="" with no character devices; already-running containers are untouched. Consumer adapters: Pod env[].value cannot expand plugin-injected variables, and HIXL or NIXL consumers require their own startup adapters. RDMA quota limits Kueue’s ResourceFlavors and gpustack-node-devices check do not meter device.gpustack.ai/rdma* or vpc.amazonaws.com/efa. Over-subscribed Workloads therefore become Admitted in Kueue while their Pods wait Pending in kube-scheduler:
Match GPU and RDMA ratios: Requesting 1 endpoint per accelerator keeps accelerator quota aligned with physical NIC count (exclusive rdma exhausts in 1 claim per NIC versus 64 on rdma.shared). Monitor Pending Pods: Alert on Pending Pods owned by Admitted Workloads rather than queue depth alone. Selection policy DevicesRDMASelectionPolicy (rdmasel, cluster-scoped) filters which HCAs and physical ports the RDMA device plugin advertises as healthy on matched Nodes. Policy updates apply immediately to new allocations (marking excluded tokens Unhealthy) without draining Nodes or restarting running containers.
To restrict an 8-GPU host with 13 verbs devices (mlx5_0..mlx5_3 slow IB, mlx5_4..mlx5_11 GPU-local 800 Gb/s IB, mlx5_12 management Ethernet) to mlx5_4..mlx5_11, set either include or exclude (never both):
yamlCopy apiVersion: worker.gpustack.ai/v1 kind: DevicesRDMASelectionPolicy # cluster-scoped, short name rdmasel metadata: name: b300-compute-hcas spec: nodeSelector: # required, non-null; {} matches all Nodes matchLabels: gpu.gpustack.ai/model: b300 include: # optional non-empty list of exact PF/VF HCA names (mutually exclusive with exclude) - mlx5_4 - mlx5_5 - mlx5_6 - mlx5_7 - mlx5_8 - mlx5_9 - mlx5_10 - mlx5_11 # exclude: # alternative to include; omit or set null when unused (never []) # - mlx5_0 # - mlx5_12 Remove an HCA or pin a 1-based physical RDMA port across all selected HCAs by patching the policy:
diffCopy apiVersion: worker.gpustack.ai/v1 kind: DevicesRDMASelectionPolicy metadata: name: b300-compute-hcas spec: nodeSelector: matchLabels: gpu.gpustack.ai/model: b300 include: - mlx5_4 - mlx5_5 - mlx5_6 - mlx5_7 - mlx5_8 - mlx5_9 - mlx5_10 - - mlx5_11 + port: 1 # optional 1-based port; every selected HCA on matched Nodes must expose it Verify resolution on the policy and each Node’s Devices status:
bashCopy kubectl get rdmasel b300-compute-hcas -o yaml kubectl get devices <node-name> -o yaml yamlCopy apiVersion: worker.gpustack.ai/v1 kind: Devices metadata: name: b300-node-0 status: interfaces: rdmaSelectionPolicy: policyRef: name: b300-compute-hcas uid: example-policy-uid generation: 1 excluded: - name: mlx5_0 reason: ExcludedByPolicy conditions: - type: RDMASelectionResolved status: "True" reason: PolicyResolved Fail-closed rules: If multiple policies match one Node, both include and exclude are set, a named HCA (or wildcards/port suffixes) is absent from a matched Node’s verbs inventory, or a selected HCA lacks port, that Node sets RDMASelectionResolved to False or Unknown and marks all RDMA tokens Unhealthy. Omit unused include / exclude fields rather than writing [].
Enabling NUMA alignment Step 1: Check kubelet policy Kubelet defaults topologyManagerPolicy to none. Confirm your Kubernetes distribution allows editing kubelet configuration before relying on NUMA alignment.
Step 2: Configure alignment Set topologyManagerPolicy: restricted and topologyManagerScope: container in KubeletConfiguration (via /var/lib/kubelet/config.yaml, your distribution’s kubelet drop-in directory, or --topology-manager-policy):
yamlCopy apiVersion: kubelet.config.k8s.io/v1beta1 kind: KubeletConfiguration topologyManagerPolicy: restricted # aligns single-socket Pods and admits multi-socket 8-GPU Pods topologyManagerScope: container # default; aligns GPU and RDMA requests inside each container Prefer restricted over single-numa-node: single-numa-node rejects any container spanning two sockets (such as an 8-GPU job on a dual-socket host) with terminal TopologyAffinityError. See Result format for all four policies.
Step 3: Drain node, restart kubelet Drain the Node before restarting kubelet so existing Pods admitted under none are not rejected in place after restart.
Verification Kubelet policy check Read the live effective kubelet configuration via nodes/proxy (configz includes defaults, whereas device-manager preflight reports unknown when no file explicitly sets a policy):
bashCopy kubectl get --raw /api/v1/nodes/<node>/proxy/configz | jq -r '.kubeletconfig | {topologyManagerPolicy, topologyManagerScope}' NIC record inspection When a Node loses feature.gpustack.ai/rdma.capable=true or stops scheduling RDMA Pods, inspect node labels and the Devices NIC inventory:
bashCopy kubectl get nodes -l feature.gpustack.ai/rdma.capable=true kubectl get devices <node> -o json | jq '[.spec.interfaces[] | (., (.virtualFunctions // [])[])] | map(select(.rdma or .link)) | map({name, pciBusId, rdmaDevice, link})' Healthy (rdma.capable=true): At least one physical NIC or SR-IOV VF reports link.state OK or Unverified (or rdma: true without a link verdict). Missing (rdma.capable absent): Every endpoint reports link.state: Failed (with port state and firstSeen) or has no bound rdmaDevice. Recovery: Repair physical links, transceivers, or the IB subnet manager on Failed ports, verify verbs driver binding when rdmaDevice is absent, and run device-manager preflight on the host. EFA engine images Official GPUStack runner images carry standard Mooncake wheels without EFA support (while the -cpu KV cache backend image already includes EFA). Granting an EFA device to a standard runner causes verbs CQ creation to fail with Operation not supported.
For any vLLM role transferring KV over EFA (via an EFA store pool or aws-efa-enabled: true direct transfer; see Engine Compatibility ), build a custom image and set it on roles[].image.
Image build dockerfileCopy FROM gpustack/runner:cuda13.0-vllm0.29.0 SHELL ["/bin/bash", "-eo", "pipefail", "-c"] ARG AWS_EFA_VERSION=1.44.0 RUN curl --retry 3 --retry-connrefused -fL "https://efa-installer.amazonaws.com/aws-efa-installer-${AWS_EFA_VERSION}.tar.gz" | tar -zx -C /tmp \ && cd /tmp/aws-efa-installer && ./efa_installer.sh -y --skip-kmod \ && rm -f /opt/amazon/efa/lib/libfabric.a && ldconfig \ && rm -rf /tmp/aws-efa-installer /var/cache/apt /var/lib/apt/lists/* ENV PATH="${PATH}:/opt/amazon/efa/bin" # Use mooncake-transfer-engine-efa on CUDA 12 bases. RUN python3 -m pip uninstall -y mooncake-transfer-engine mooncake-transfer-engine-cuda13 \ && python3 -m pip install --no-cache-dir --no-deps mooncake-transfer-engine-efa-cuda13==0.3.13.post1 Verify EfaTransport inside the built image and in engine startup logs:
bashCopy MC="$(python3 -c 'import importlib.util as u; print(u.find_spec("mooncake").submodule_search_locations[0])')" grep -ac EfaTransport "$MC/engine.so" kubectl logs <engine-pod> | grep 'The Mooncake Transfer Engine is using efa' Image maintenance Rebuild roles[].image whenever upgrading the runner base, libfabric, or the Mooncake minor line (Version compatibility ).
Limitations x86_64 vLLM only: No aarch64 EFA wheel is published, intra-node NVLink is omitted, and SGLang extensions are absent. Fail-fast without EFA: Requesting efa on a Node without EFA hardware fails instead of falling back to TCP (tcp and rdma protocols still work). InfiniBand/RoCE data paths with the bundled rdma-core are unmeasured. SGLang and EFA SGLang does not support EFA on either direct or store KV paths (direct interface requests without another fabric are refused at admission, and EFA wheels lack SGLang modules). Run SGLang over TCP on AWS.
AWS fabric choices Use EFA (vpc.amazonaws.com/efa) or TCP on AWS EFA instances; device.gpustack.ai/rdma* allocatable counts remain 0 on EFA-only hosts.
Troubleshooting Symptom Signal Resolution RDMA key absent on all Nodes Zero allocatable device.gpustack.ai/rdma* Verify verbs hardware and Device Manager --no-shared / --no-partitioned flags. Key present, 0 allocatable Link Failed or RDMASelectionResolved!=True Check Selection policy and NIC record inspection . Workload Admitted, Pod Pending Unmet device.gpustack.ai/rdma* in scheduler events Free RDMA endpoints or switch to rdma.shared (RDMA quota limits ). Pod fails with TopologyAffinityError Kubelet rejects cross-socket allocation Use topologyManagerPolicy: restricted and keep GPU and RDMA requests in one container. Fewer /dev/infiniband entries than requested Shared HCA tokens deduplicated Count uverbs<N> nodes (rdma_cm appears once); check Injected devices . Node loses rdma.capable label All NIC/VF links Failed Run NIC record inspection and repair physical links. See also — Accelerator Requests (Pod request rules and co-location conditions) · RDMA Networking Walkthrough (end-to-end endpoint verification) · Preflight Checks (bare-host RDMA link and kubelet topology checks)
Next → Preflight Checks — validate node hardware, slicing, and RDMA links before workloads arrive.
title: RDMA Operations

content:
Topology GPUStack models failure and fabric domains (regions, zones, racks, and network switches) so Kueue topology-aware scheduling (TAS) places multi-Pod replica groups inside a single domain.
Contents Overview Configuration Operations Troubleshooting Overview Placement and scheduling A TopologySource selects a node inventory source and an ordered label hierarchy (without one, managed queues use a hostname-only default profile). The worker publishes Kueue Topology resources and binds them to ResourceFlavors and ClusterQueues.
Configuration Topology sources Choose one inventory source in Topology inventory sources , then configure Topograph , existing Node labels , a ConfigMap snapshot , or a webhook snapshot .
Operations Step 1: Select source Pick the single inventory source that owns hierarchy labels for your Nodes.
Step 2: Apply source Create the TopologySource (and any backing ConfigMap or HTTPS credentials).
Step 3: Verify placement Confirm profile labels, Kueue Topology objects, and ClusterQueue readiness in Verification , then constrain serving roles in Topology level requests or follow the Hierarchical Placement Walkthrough .
Troubleshooting When replicas remain Pending, follow Diagnose Pending workloads to compare requested topology levels, per-domain capacity, and profile alignment.
See also — RDMA Networking (NIC endpoints) · Model Deployment (multi-Pod serving roles)
Next → Topology-Aware Scheduling Operations — publish domain hierarchies and diagnose TAS placement.
title: Topology

content:
Topology-Aware Scheduling Operations Configure TopologySource inventories for fresh managed queues, constrain replica placement with Kueue topology-aware scheduling (TAS), update live hierarchies safely, and diagnose Pending PodSets. Legacy non-TAS queues from earlier releases are not migrated automatically.
Contents Topology inventory sources Topology level requests Live hierarchy changes Verification Troubleshooting Topology inventory sources Assign at most one Ready TopologySource per Node. Zero or multiple matching Ready sources fall back to the hostname-only profile so conflicting hierarchies never merge.
Scenario Inventory source Bundled Topograph supports your cloud, fabric, DRA, or on-prem topology Enable topograph in Helm values and read its labels with nodeLabels. Cloud provider or admin already labels Nodes Use nodeLabels (read-only). Inventory is exported as a versioned document Publish YAML/JSON in a ConfigMap and use configMap. External inventory service serves snapshots Serve authenticated HTTPS JSON/YAML and use webhook. Declare only strictly nested trees (every rack belongs to one zone, and every zone to one region); independent axes such as rack and MIG partition do not form a valid hierarchy.
Topograph setup Topograph is disabled by default. Enable it on Kubernetes 1.27+ with a supported provider and the k8s engine. For private clusters, override topograph.image.repository, imagePullSecrets, and topograph.config.credentialsSecret:
yamlCopy topograph: enabled: true provider: name: aws params: {} engine: name: k8s params: {} nodeDataBroker: enabled: true nodeSelector: # optional; restrict DaemonSet to NVIDIA PCI Nodes feature.node.kubernetes.io/pci-10de.present: "true" On AWS, set the EC2 IMDSv2 hop limit to >= 2 for node-data-broker and grant ec2:DescribeInstanceTopology to the Topograph API ServiceAccount (topograph_aws_pod_identity_enabled=true in the repository EKS Terraform module).
Once Topograph labels Nodes, expose the actual published tiers from broadest to narrowest via a read-only TopologySource:
yamlCopy apiVersion: worker.gpustack.ai/v1 kind: TopologySource # cluster-scoped metadata: name: cloud-fabric spec: nodeSelector: {} # {} matches every Node levels: # 1..16 unique keys, broadest to narrowest; kubernetes.io/hostname appended automatically - topology.kubernetes.io/region - topology.kubernetes.io/zone - fabric.topograph.run/tier-2 - fabric.topograph.run/tier-1 nodeLabels: {} # read-only inventory mode The worker takes the longest populated prefix on each Node, normalizes contiguous Topograph tiers coarsest-to-finest, appends kubernetes.io/hostname, and hashes the key list into topology.gpustack.ai/profile.
Existing Node labels Use nodeLabels when another controller or cloud provider already writes Node labels:
yamlCopy apiVersion: worker.gpustack.ai/v1 kind: TopologySource metadata: name: cloud-zones spec: nodeSelector: matchLabels: node-role.kubernetes.io/worker: "" levels: - topology.kubernetes.io/region - topology.kubernetes.io/zone nodeLabels: {} Condition Reason Resolution Duplicate key in levels Levels must be unique Remove the repeated label key. Child label present without parent Broken parent chain on Node Populate every ancestor label (missing fine suffixes are allowed). kubernetes.io/hostname in levels Reserved implicit leaf level Remove kubernetes.io/hostname from levels. ConfigMap snapshot Store a TopologySourceConfiguration YAML or JSON document in the worker namespace (gpustack-system):
yamlCopy apiVersion: worker.gpustack.ai/v1alpha1 kind: TopologySourceConfiguration revision: inventory-42 nodes: worker-a: topology.gpustack.ai/region: region-a topology.gpustack.ai/zone: zone-a topology.gpustack.ai/rack: rack-01 worker-b: topology.gpustack.ai/region: region-a topology.gpustack.ai/zone: zone-a topology.gpustack.ai/rack: rack-02 --- apiVersion: worker.gpustack.ai/v1 kind: TopologySource metadata: name: data-center spec: nodeSelector: {} levels: - topology.gpustack.ai/region - topology.gpustack.ai/zone - topology.gpustack.ai/rack configMap: configMapRef: namespace: gpustack-system # must be the worker namespace name: topology-inventory key: snapshot.yaml maxStaleness: 10m # retains last valid NodeFeature on read failure until expiry Snapshots validate atomically: unknown Nodes, undeclared keys, broken parent chains, or read-only topology.kubernetes.io/{region,zone} mismatches reject the revision. Valid snapshots write one NFD NodeFeature per Node; set additionalWritePrefix (topology.example.com/) for custom DNS prefixes (reserved prefixes are refused).
Webhook snapshot Serve the TopologySourceConfiguration payload (<= 1 MiB) over authenticated HTTPS (GET, redirects and proxies disabled) using worker-namespace credentials:
yamlCopy apiVersion: worker.gpustack.ai/v1 kind: TopologySource metadata: name: inventory-service spec: nodeSelector: {} levels: - topology.gpustack.ai/rack webhook: url: https://topology-inventory.gpustack-system.svc/snapshot # required HTTPS URL without embedded auth pollInterval: 1m # positive duration; must be >= timeout timeout: 10s # positive duration maxStaleness: 5m # positive duration caBundleConfigMapRef: namespace: gpustack-system name: topology-inventory-ca # key: ca.crt bearerTokenSecretRef: # set exactly one of bearerTokenSecretRef (key: token) or tlsClientCertificateSecretRef (tls.crt/tls.key) namespace: gpustack-system name: topology-inventory-token Restrict TopologySource and credential RBAC to cluster administrators and scope egress to the inventory endpoint.
Topology level requests Set roles[].topology.requiredLevel to a configured label key (never a bare word like zone or a concrete zone value) so all size Pods of each replica fit inside one domain:
diffCopy apiVersion: worker.gpustack.ai/v1 kind: ModelDeployment metadata: name: zoned-deployment namespace: team-a spec: roles: - name: decode replicas: 2 size: 4 + topology: + requiredLevel: topology.kubernetes.io/zone Omit requiredLevel for unconstrained placement (kubernetes.io/hostname is implicit; see Topology placement ). Editing requiredLevel updates the role hash and rolls only that role’s replicas.
Live hierarchy changes Updating levels creates a new profile and Topology. Once Nodes and Devices converge, the operator creates replacement ResourceFlavors, drains the ClusterQueue (HoldAndDrain), swaps flavors at zero reservations, and restores the stop policy.
If TopologyReady=False, inspect its reason and migration annotations before editing again. Missing flavors, quota mismatches, or exceeding 64 flavors per resource group preserve the previous queue plan.
Verification Inspect the source, Node profile labels, Kueue Topology objects, ResourceFlavors, and ClusterQueue conditions:
bashCopy kubectl get topologysources.worker.gpustack.ai kubectl get nodes -L topology.gpustack.ai/profile,topology.kubernetes.io/zone kubectl get topologies.kueue.x-k8s.io kubectl get resourceflavors.kueue.x-k8s.io -o yaml kubectl get clusterqueues.kueue.x-k8s.io -o yaml For ConfigMap or webhook sources, also verify generated NFD NodeFeature objects (refresh the snapshot if Node selector labels change later):
bashCopy source_uid=$(kubectl get topologysource data-center -o jsonpath='{.metadata.uid}') kubectl -n gpustack-system get nodefeatures -l "topology.gpustack.ai/source-uid=$source_uid" -o yaml Confirm TopologySource is Ready and every managed Node and Devices object shares one topology.gpustack.ai/profile. Verify each ResourceFlavor ends in kubernetes.io/hostname and ClusterQueue TopologyReady is True; inspect topologyRequest.required and topologyAssignment on Workloads.
EKS zone verification The repository EKS fixture provisions two CPU node groups across two zones (two Nodes per zone) with topograph_aws_pod_identity_enabled=true. A size-2 PodSet schedules within one zone, while a size-3 PodSet stays Pending across four total Nodes. Review AWS pricing before apply, test on fresh queues, and destroy all billable resources afterward.
Troubleshooting Diagnose Pending workloads bashCopy kubectl -n <ns> get modeldeployments.worker.gpustack.ai <name> -o jsonpath='{.status}' | jq kubectl -n <ns> get workloads.kueue.x-k8s.io -o yaml kubectl get clusterqueues.kueue.x-k8s.io <cq> -o jsonpath='{.status.conditions}' | jq kubectl get nodes -L topology.gpustack.ai/profile Symptom Signal Next action Replica stays Pending Workload QuotaReserved=False with topologyRequest.required set Free capacity inside a single domain at that level (e.g., 2 Nodes/zone cannot fit a 3-Pod zone group) or relax requiredLevel. Aggregate capacity exists, no fit Mixed topology.gpustack.ai/profile labels across candidate Nodes Align TopologySource selectors so all pool Nodes publish the same profile. One role reserved, Pods gated Workload QuotaReserved=True, joint check Pending (or Parked after 30m) Free sibling role capacity in a valid domain, or recreate/reactivate Parked deployments. Queue blocks admission ClusterQueue TopologyReady=False or Unknown (AwaitingQueueStatus) Check flavor profiles, Kueue Active status, and keep flavors <= 64 per resource group. Source not applied TopologySource Ready=False (Valid or OwnershipConflict) Fix broken parent chains, snapshot errors, or overlapping TopologySource selectors. See also — Hierarchical Placement Walkthrough (end-to-end zone and rack placement) · Model Deployment Configuration (roles[].topology.requiredLevel contract) · Installation Modes (bundled Topograph chart ownership)
Next → Model Deployment Configuration — configure multi-member serving roles for topology-aware placement.
title: Topology-Aware Scheduling Operations

content:
High Availability Operations Every control-plane component in the chart elects a single active leader, so extra replicas provide failover rather than higher reconciliation throughput. Enable high availability in values.yaml by raising control-plane replica counts and enabling disruption budgets; node agents (Device Managers, NFD worker, and CSI node DaemonSets) already run one Pod per node.
Contents Prerequisites Configuration External worker webhook limits Verification Prerequisites A DoNotSchedule spread requires at least as many schedulable Nodes as your largest replica count, or surplus Pods stay Pending. The example below targets three replicas across three Nodes; on smaller clusters, lower replica counts or switch to ScheduleAnyway.
Control-plane components tolerate standard control-plane taints and no others (including cordon taints), so drained Pods reschedule elsewhere. If your Nodes carry custom taints, add them to each component’s tolerations.
If you are upgrading from an older release where Kueue controller manager, NFD master, and NFD GC tolerated all taints, add explicit tolerations first and run helm upgrade with --reset-then-reuse-values rather than --reuse-values; see Upgrading the Chart .
Configuration Save these values as ha.yaml and apply them with helm upgrade (chart mode is required because image mode exposes no subchart values):
yamlCopy worker: replicas: 3 podDisruptionBudget: enabled: true minAvailable: 2 topologySpreadConstraints: # labelSelector auto-populated when omitted; worker.affinity replaces default - maxSkew: 1 topologyKey: kubernetes.io/hostname whenUnsatisfiable: DoNotSchedule kueue: controllerManager: replicas: 3 podDisruptionBudget: enabled: true minAvailable: 2 topologySpreadConstraints: # explicit labelSelector required; chart has no affinity key - maxSkew: 1 topologyKey: kubernetes.io/hostname whenUnsatisfiable: DoNotSchedule labelSelector: matchLabels: app.kubernetes.io/name: kueue control-plane: controller-manager node-feature-discovery: master: replicaCount: 3 # auto-enables -enable-leader-election above 1 podDisruptionBudget: enable: true # NFD key is "enable", not "enabled" minAvailable: 2 # affinity: {} # optional; replaces NFD's default control-plane preference csi-driver-nfs: controller: replicas: 2 strategyType: RollingUpdate # overrides Recreate default; chart has no PDB topologySpreadConstraints: # required >1 replica due to hostNetwork port bind - maxSkew: 1 topologyKey: kubernetes.io/hostname whenUnsatisfiable: DoNotSchedule labelSelector: matchLabels: app: csi-nfs-controller csi-driver-s3: controller: replicas: 2 # process-level failover only; chart has no PDB or spread field strategyType: RollingUpdate bashCopy helm upgrade gpustack-operator gpustack/gpustack-operator \ --namespace gpustack-system --reset-then-reuse-values --values ha.yaml Worker control plane Only the elected worker leader runs controllers, while every replica serves the aggregated extension API (instancetypes, devices) and admission webhooks. Running one replica makes node loss block API reads and Pod admission until reschedule.
Node spread belongs in worker.topologySpreadConstraints. By default, worker.affinity sets preferred Pod anti-affinity so three replicas still start on two Nodes; setting worker.affinity replaces that default entirely.
Kueue controller manager Standby Kueue replicas do not reconcile, but every replica serves Kueue’s webhooks (failurePolicy: Fail). Losing a single-replica Kueue node blocks Pod creation across every Kueue-managed namespace.
Always include labelSelector in kueue.controllerManager.topologySpreadConstraints; without it, Kubernetes counts every Pod in the namespace.
NFD master While NFD master is unavailable, existing labels and running workloads remain intact, and only new or changed Nodes pause classification. Keep NFD GC at one replica, because brief GC downtime only delays cleanup of deleted Node records.
NFD spells its disruption budget switch enable (enabled: true is ignored) and supports placement only through node-feature-discovery.master.affinity.
NFS and S3 controllers CSI controller outages delay new volume provisioning, resizing, and snapshots while mounted volumes continue running through the CSI node DaemonSets. Both bundled CSI charts omit PodDisruptionBudget templates, honor controller.affinity only when nodeSelectorTerms is set, and default strategyType to Recreate unless overridden to RollingUpdate.
On csi-driver-nfs, DoNotSchedule hostname spread is mandatory above one replica because controller Pods use hostNetwork and collide on the liveness port if co-located. csi-driver-s3 exposes no spread field, so two replicas provide process-level failover without guaranteed node separation.
External worker webhook limits When an image-mode worker runs outside the target cluster on an adjacent network (!LoopbackKubeInside && LoopbackKubeNearby), its webhooks register against a single node IP URL rather than a Kubernetes Service. Standby replicas receive no webhook traffic, so keep that topology at one replica. Chart-mode webhooks always route through an in-cluster Service.
Verification Confirm that all control-plane Deployments, disruption budgets, node placements, and leader elections are healthy:
bashCopy NS=gpustack-system # 1. Every control-plane Deployment reports all replicas Ready: kubectl -n "$NS" get deploy # 2. Disruption budgets exist with ALLOWED DISRUPTIONS >= 1: kubectl -n "$NS" get pdb # 3. Replicas run on distinct Nodes: kubectl -n "$NS" get pods --field-selector status.phase=Running \ -o custom-columns='POD:.metadata.name,NODE:.spec.nodeName' # 4. NFD master elected a leader: kubectl -n "$NS" logs deploy/node-feature-discovery-master | grep -i "leader" Test failover by draining the Node hosting the active worker leader and confirming uninterrupted API reads:
bashCopy kubectl drain <node> --ignore-daemonsets --delete-emptydir-data kubectl -n "$NS" rollout status deploy/gpustack-operator-worker kubectl get instancetypes kubectl uncordon <node> See also — Installation Modes (HA values require chart mode) · KV Cache Election and Failover (leader election on KVCacheBackend custom resources)
Next → NVIDIA MIG Operations — configure and verify MIG partition lifecycles.
title: High Availability Operations

content:
Installation Modes GPUStack Operator installs its dependencies in chart mode or image mode. Chart mode renders bundled subcharts inside one Helm release; image mode lets an external worker install its packaged chart at runtime. Choose one mode per cluster.
Contents Prerequisites Chart and image modes Installation ownership conflicts Configuration Settings and precedence Worker-managed resources Prerequisites The Helm chart accepts Kubernetes 1.23 and newer. Use Kubernetes 1.29 or newer for the Kueue scheduling chain and node model delivery. Model Image Source requires newer Kubernetes and container-runtime versions.
Chart and image modes Kueue, NFD, Topograph, and the NFS and S3 CSI drivers ship under deploy/gpustack-operator/chart/charts/ behind per-subchart enabled switches:
Mode Installation Chart mode Default. Helm renders the worker, Device Manager DaemonSets, and enabled subcharts in one release. The worker runs with --disable-applications=* (worker.disableApplications, default ["*"]) and installs no Helm release at runtime. Image mode No Helm release deploys the worker. An external worker installs ${GPUSTACK_CONF_DIR:-/etc/gpustack}/charts/gpustack-operator-<version>.tgz as release gpustack-operator-device-manager1. In image mode, the worker generates its values overlay (worker.enabled=false, fullnameOverride: gpustack-operator, component switches, and manufacturer map) from flags and settings, so subchart fields such as kueue.controllerManager.replicas cannot be customized there.
--disable-applications accepts *, kueue, node-feature-discovery, csi-driver-nfs, csi-driver-s3, device-manager, model-manager, and model-transfer.
Two components sit outside --disable-applications:
gpustack-cpu-info: the worker always applies this NodeFeatureRule, including when node-feature-discovery.enabled=false hands feature discovery to an existing NFD installation. Topograph: disabled by default and configurable only in chart mode because it requires provider credentials and trust settings. TopologySource snapshots and hostname fallback work without it (Topology-Aware Scheduling Operations ). Installation ownership conflicts Both modes render the same chart under fullnameOverride: gpustack-operator. Enabling a component in both modes creates identically named objects, and Helm rejects adoption with invalid ownership metadata, blocking worker startup.
Do not split components across chart mode and image mode either; keeping enabled flags and worker.disableApplications synchronized across upgrades has no safeguard. Keep worker.disableApplications: ["*"] whenever Helm deploys the worker.
Configuration Use these chart switches to scope what chart mode deploys:
deviceManager.enabled=false: omits Device Manager DaemonSets (for control-plane-only installs). With worker.disableApplications: ["*"], the worker does not install them at runtime. modelManager.enabled=false: omits the Model Manager DaemonSet, CSIDriver, and Node delivery defaults (Model Store Operations ). modelTransfer.enabled=false: omits remote-delivery DaemonSets, Services, RBAC, TLS Secrets, and source-ledger mounts, and sets GPUSTACK_MODEL_ARTIFACT_REMOTE_DELIVERY_POLICY=Disabled on the worker (Remote Weight Delivery ). worker.enabled=false: deploys only node and subchart components (used by image mode’s runtime overlay). Settings and precedence Runtime Setting objects (gpustack.ai/v1, short name set, backed by Secret/gpustack-settings in gpustack-system) can be patched live with kubectl -n gpustack-system patch setting <name> --type merge -p '{"spec":{"value":"..."}}'. On every worker start, restart, or upgrade, the worker reconciles each Setting in four ordered rules:
Rule Precedence Behavior 1. Backfill Missing key only Seeds an absent Setting from GPUSTACK_<UPPER_SNAKE_NAME> if set, else the built-in default. 2. env-declared Wins on every start Any non-blank GPUSTACK_* variable on the worker Deployment (from global.imageRegistry, global.imagePullPolicy, modelManager.enabled, modelTransfer.enabled, or worker.env) overwrites the stored Setting. 3. default-tracked Wins if unclaimed by env If settings-default-tracking lists the Setting (built-in image Settings are tracked by default), the built-in default overwrites the stored value on start. 4. Administrator-owned Preserved Every other Setting keeps its stored value across restarts and upgrades. Reverted setting after restart If a patched Setting reverts after a worker restart or upgrade, inspect which startup rule overwrote it:
bashCopy # 1. Read worker startup override logs (prints rule="env-declared" or rule="default-tracked" and envName): kubectl -n gpustack-system logs deploy/gpustack-operator-worker | grep 'setting overridden on start' # 2. Inspect non-blank GPUSTACK_* variables on the worker Deployment: kubectl -n gpustack-system get deploy gpustack-operator-worker -o yaml | grep -A1 'GPUSTACK_' # 3. Inspect settings-default-tracking: kubectl -n gpustack-system get setting settings-default-tracking -o yaml rule="env-declared": update or clear the owning Helm value (an empty string "" releases env ownership) or worker.env entry, then run helm upgrade. rule="default-tracked": remove that Setting name from settings-default-tracking with kubectl -n gpustack-system patch setting settings-default-tracking --type merge -p '{"spec":{"value":"<remaining-comma-separated-names>"}}', then re-apply your Setting value. Worker-managed resources Helm validates REST mappings for the entire render before creating objects, so a chart cannot render a custom resource whose CRD is templated in the same install or supplied externally. Instead, the worker applies these objects after their CRDs become established:
gpustack-node-devices and gpustack-model-deployment-joint AdmissionChecks: created in both modes once Kueue’s templated CRDs exist, and marked Active before queues reference them. gpustack-cpu-info NodeFeatureRule: applied once NFD’s CRD exists, including when node-feature-discovery.enabled=false omits bundled NFD CRDs. AdmissionCheck Purpose Referencing queues gpustack-node-devices Verifies per-accelerator fit before placement Accelerated queues while instance-type-derived-from-node is true gpustack-model-deployment-joint Holds multi-role ModelDeployment replicas for atomic gang admission Every operator-managed queue, including CPU and custom InstanceType queues gpustack-model-deployment-joint passes single-role deployments and standalone workloads immediately.
The worker also installs and updates its own CRDs, aggregated APIServices, and webhook configurations at startup while preserving status, so helm template omits them and helm uninstall leaves them behind. Kueue’s AdmissionChecks are removed with Kueue’s CRDs, and deploy/gpustack-operator/chart/files/cleanup.sh deletes gpustack-cpu-info while it retains app.kubernetes.io/part-of: gpustack-operator.
See also — Migrating to Bundled Subcharts (transferring ownership from legacy runtime releases) · High Availability Operations (multi-replica control-plane configuration) · Topology-Aware Scheduling Operations (Topograph and generic topology sources)
Next → High Availability Operations — configure control-plane replicas and disruption budgets.
Image mode retains the historical gpustack-operator-device-manager release name so existing image-mode clusters upgrade in place. ↩︎
title: Installation Modes

content:
Migrating to Bundled Subcharts Through v0.7.x, the Helm chart deployed only the worker and Device Managers while the worker installed four separate Helm releases at runtime:
Legacy runtime release Bundled subchart gpustack-kueue kueue gpustack-node-feature-discovery node-feature-discovery gpustack-csi-driver-nfs csi-driver-nfs gpustack-csi-driver-s3 csi-driver-s3 Current releases bundle all four as subcharts under one values.yaml with worker.disableApplications: ["*"]. Helm adopts existing resources in place, preserving live ClusterQueues, Workloads, ResourceFlavors, Node labels, and mounted volumes.
Contents Helm ownership transfer Upgrade hooks Automatic image-mode migration Troubleshooting Chart configuration and cleanup Rollback data loss Verification Helm ownership transfer Before upgrading, snapshot your scheduling chain (see Rollback data loss ), then upgrade with Helm 3.21+ and --take-ownership1:
bashCopy helm repo add gpustack https://docs.gpustack.ai/gpustack-operator/charts helm repo update helm upgrade gpustack-operator gpustack/gpustack-operator \ --namespace gpustack-system \ --take-ownership Pass --take-ownership only once so Helm can import objects owned by the four legacy releases. Omit the flag on subsequent upgrades so Helm does not adopt unrelated hand-created resources.
Release and namespace identity Keep release name gpustack-operator and your existing namespace (gpustack-system by default):
Release name: gpustack-operator-worker and gpustack-operator-device-manager-<manufacturer> derive their names from the release, whereas bundled subcharts pin fixed names via fullnameOverride. Namespace: Helm cannot move an installed release across namespaces. Fresh installs can use any namespace except one matched by Kueue’s managedJobsNamespaceSelector. Upgrade hooks Two idempotent hook Jobs run during helm upgrade (skipped only if you pass --no-hooks):
pre-upgrade / pre-install: clears any Terminating Kueue CRD deadlock (deleting Kueue webhook configurations before stripping kueue.x-k8s.io/resource-in-use finalizers) and applies subchart crds/ updates that Helm normally skips on upgrade. post-upgrade: deletes the four legacy Helm release Secrets (kubectl delete secret -l owner=helm,name=<release>) without uninstalling their adopted objects, then prunes obsolete legacy objects while preserving CRDs, PersistentVolumes, and PersistentVolumeClaims. Never run helm uninstall gpustack-kueue manually; uninstalling a legacy release deletes the objects the operator release just adopted. Confirm that only one release remains:
bashCopy helm list -n gpustack-system Automatic image-mode migration In image mode, the worker detects its own legacy runtime release Secrets and enables ownership transfer automatically for that single upgrade. No manual command is required.
Troubleshooting Helm hooks adopt only prior Helm releases. If Kueue or NFD was installed from raw manifests, kustomize, or another operator, choose one of two paths:
Collision symptoms: Helm rejects unowned Kueue CRDs with invalid ownership metadata (NFD’s crds/ skip when present). Worse, a manifest-installed Kueue in kueue-system does not collide on namespaced objects, so forcing --take-ownership leaves two Kueue controllers reconciling the same Workloads. Option 1: Keep the external Kueue and NFD when other workloads depend on them:
bashCopy helm upgrade --install gpustack-operator gpustack/gpustack-operator \ --namespace gpustack-system --create-namespace \ --set kueue.enabled=false --set node-feature-discovery.enabled=false The worker still applies gpustack-cpu-info against your existing NFD. Keep both components at operator-compatible versions.
Option 2: Hand Kueue over to the chart by deleting the external Kueue’s Deployments, Services, RBAC, and webhook configurations (failurePolicy: Fail), keep its CRDs intact, and stamp Helm ownership on those CRDs before installing:
bashCopy for crd in $(kubectl get crd -o name | grep 'kueue\.x-k8s\.io'); do kubectl label "$crd" app.kubernetes.io/managed-by=Helm --overwrite kubectl annotate "$crd" meta.helm.sh/release-name=gpustack-operator \ meta.helm.sh/release-namespace=gpustack-system --overwrite done Review Rollback data loss first, because the chart release then owns Kueue’s CRDs.
Chart configuration and cleanup Manufacturer configuration Top-level manufacturers moved to global.manufacturers so both the operator chart and bundled Kueue read one identity map:
yamlCopy global: manufacturers: nvidia: pciVendorID: "10de" resourceName: nvidia.com/gpu runtimeName: nvidia runtimeInjectsDriver: true partitionKind: mig Default values moved automatically. If you customized top-level manufacturers, migrate those entries under global.manufacturers and delete the old key so Device Managers do not fall back to defaults.
The chart creates RuntimeClass objects only where runtimeInjectsDriver or runtimeInjectsDevices is true (ascend, iluvatar, mthreads, nvidia, and no longer amd). Set deviceManager.createRuntimeClasses=false to opt out.
Certificate configuration worker.certmanager moved to global.certmanager (default enabled: auto) and now governs both the worker and bundled Kueue:
yamlCopy global: certmanager: enabled: auto # enum: auto, true, false issuer: name: "" # optional; covers both worker and Kueue without creating self-signed Issuers kind: Issuer On clusters with cert-manager installed, auto switches Kueue from self-managed webhook certificates to cert-manager Certificates and cainjector CA bundles. To keep self-managed certificates across all components, pass --set global.certmanager.enabled=false in the migration helm upgrade (legacy worker.certmanager values are ignored).
Disabling cert-manager Enabling cert-manager later requires no extra steps. Disabling cert-manager after it was active fails a plain helm upgrade twice: Helm rejects Secret/kueue-webhook-server-cert on missing ownership metadata, and visibility.kueue.x-k8s.io APIServices reject insecureSkipTLSVerify: true while cainjector’s caBundle remains set.
Switch cleanly from cert-manager to self-managed certificates in two steps:
bashCopy # 1. Delete Kueue visibility APIServices carrying cainjector CA bundles (recreated by the upgrade): kubectl delete apiservice v1beta1.visibility.kueue.x-k8s.io v1beta2.visibility.kueue.x-k8s.io # 2. Adopt kueue-webhook-server-cert with Helm 3.21+: helm upgrade gpustack-operator <chart> --namespace gpustack-system --reset-then-reuse-values \ --set global.certmanager.enabled=false --take-ownership --wait If cert-manager may be installed or removed independently, pin global.certmanager.enabled to true or false rather than auto.
Kueue removal on uninstall Because the operator release now templates Kueue’s CRDs, helm uninstall gpustack-operator deletes every ClusterQueue, LocalQueue, ResourceFlavor, AdmissionCheck, and Workload in the cluster. Set --set kueue.enabled=false if other workloads share Kueue.
Leftover certificate Secrets Older workers created one gpustack-cert-<5-char-random> Secret per restart instead of the current content-hashed gpustack-cert-<16-hex> Secret. Inspect and optionally delete unused 5-character Secrets:
bashCopy kubectl -n gpustack-system get secret | grep '^gpustack-cert-' Rollback data loss Do not run helm rollback across the subchart migration. Because pre-v0.8 revisions contain no Kueue templates and legacy release records were retired, helm rollback deletes Kueue’s templated CRDs along with every ClusterQueue, LocalQueue, ResourceFlavor, AdmissionCheck, and queued Workload (plus any custom InstanceTypes if full cleanup follows).
Snapshot your scheduling objects before upgrading:
bashCopy kubectl get clusterqueues,resourceflavors,admissionchecks,instancetypes,localqueues -A -o yaml \ > gpustack-chain.yaml If you must return to a pre-subchart version, uninstall and reinstall cleanly via Path A in Migrating from v0.5.x .
Verification Confirm single-release ownership, clean legacy labels, and intact scheduling resources:
bashCopy NS=gpustack-system # 1. Only gpustack-operator remains in Helm: helm list -n "$NS" # 2. Worker and adopted workloads are healthy under gpustack-operator: kubectl -n "$NS" rollout status deploy/gpustack-operator-worker kubectl -n "$NS" get deploy,daemonset -l app.kubernetes.io/instance=gpustack-operator -o name # 3. Zero objects retain legacy release instance labels (expect empty output for both): LEGACY='app.kubernetes.io/instance in (gpustack-kueue,gpustack-node-feature-discovery,gpustack-csi-driver-nfs,gpustack-csi-driver-s3)' kubectl get deploy,daemonset,svc,sa,cm,role,rolebinding -n "$NS" -o name -l "$LEGACY" kubectl get clusterrole,clusterrolebinding,csidriver,storageclass -o name -l "$LEGACY" # 4. Scheduling chain, Node labels, and Kueue CRDs remain healthy: kubectl get clusterqueues,resourceflavors,instancetypes,admissioncheck kubectl get workloads -A kubectl get nodes -o json | grep -c 'feature.gpustack.ai/' kubectl get crd -o custom-columns=NAME:.metadata.name,DELETING:.metadata.deletionTimestamp | grep kueue See also — Installation Modes (mode ownership and runtime settings) · High Availability Operations (replica configuration in values.yaml) · Migrating from v0.5.x (v0.5.x pool rename) · Migration Troubleshooting (recovering wedged upgrades)
Next → Installation Modes — configure chart values and runtime settings.
